The 8D approach is based on a team working together to solve a problem and comprises three types of actions:  Containment actions  Corrective actions  Preventive actions 12 Quality Notification 570 If there is a nonconformance with a quality requirement that contains a request to take appropriate action, the 8D method comprises eight problem-solving steps as shown in Figure 12.47, which is the initial screen for starting the problem-solving process using the 8D method: 1. D1 Team 2. D2 Problem Description 3. D3 Containment Actions 4. D4 Root Causes 5. D5 Defined Corrective Actions 6. D6 Implemented Corrective Actions 7. D7 Preventative Actions 8. D8 Congratulating Your Team D1 Team Let’s begin with the first step by choosing the forward arrow for the step D1 Team, caus- ing the screen shown in Figure 12.48 to appear. In this step, a team is formed to solve the problem. Figure 12.48 Creating a Team © 571 12.7 Quality Issue Resolution This team will need to have a team leader as well as a team member with their contact details to maintain effective coordination and communication. This team will be responsible ensuring all subsequent steps in 8D are completed. Figure 12.48 shows that two team members are part of the 8D process, while additional details can be main- tained in the comments. Once this step is initiated and then concluded, be sure to set the status to Set in Process followed by setting it to Complete (see Figure 12.48). Choose the Back icon at the top of Figure 12.48, and then notice that this step’s status is turned green when the step status is set to Complete (see Figure 12.49). Figure 12.49 Team Formation Completed D2 Problem Description In this step, the 8D team leader and team member clearly define the problem. Problem description will have the Defect Code Group and Defect Code. This step also displays details relating to the original source defect (see Figure 12.50). Once this step is initiated and then concluded, be sure to set the status to Set in Process followed by setting it to Complete. The step status will turn green when the step status is set to Complete. 12 Quality Notification 572 Figure 12.50 Problem Description D3 Containment Actions A containment step is immediate in nature by virtue of the tasks to be performed or actions to be taken to temporarily resolve the problem. The purpose of the contain- ment action is to ensure no further immediate problems are encountered until the cor- rective and preventive actions are put in place for a sustained solution to the problem. In this step, choose Create to create a Quality Task that is linked to the problem-solving process number. Figure 12.51 Containment Actions © 573 12.7 Quality Issue Resolution For each quality task, assign a Quality Task code and the associated Predecessor Task (see Figure 12.51). Once this step is initiated and then concluded, be sure to set the status Set in Process followed by setting it to Complete. The step status will turn green when the step status is set to Complete. D4 Root Causes In this step of the 8D process, enter a detailed description for each cause. Further, click Create to create the Cause Code linked with the Cause Code Group. Figure 12.52 shows two such root causes and the option to maintain the long text of these causes. Once this step is initiated and then concluded, be sure to set the status to Set in Process followed by setting it to Complete. The step status will turn green when the step status is set to Complete. At any time, choose Apply to add an entry during the entire 8D pro- cess, followed by choosing Save located on the bottom-left side of the screen to save the step. If needed, a step can be deleted by choosing Discard Draft. Figure 12.52 Root Causes D5 Defined Corrective Actions A corrective action is put in place to avoid recurrence of the problem and eliminate the root cause that led to the problem in the first place. In this step, you not only define the corrective actions but also take steps to implement them for each cause (see Figure 12.53). Here, choose Create Task for tasks that need to be put in place for corrective actions against each of the two root causes. In Figure 12.54, maintain the details of the quality task (corrective action) by choosing the relevant Task Code from the Task Code Group. Maintain a short Description, as well as any long text, followed by maintaining the Task Processor’s ID. Estimated Time Effort to complete the quality task of a corrective action can also be maintained. On saving this 12 Quality Notification 574 entry, the system has created quality task 89 (located on the top-left side of the screen) that we’ll use as an example to implement in the next step of the 8D process. Figure 12.53 Corrective Actions Figure 12.54 Quality Tasks © 575 12.7 Quality Issue Resolution D6 Implemented Corrective Actions The main purpose of the implemented corrective action step is to verify the actions taken in step D5. In the step, choose the radio button of the previously created Task 89 followed by choosing Implement (see Figure 12.55 1) The defined task 91 is displayed as the successor of task 89 2. Figure 12.55 Corrective Actions Figure 12.56 shows the details of the newly created task 91 along with details of the asso- ciated cause. Figure 12.56 Corrective Actions Implemented 12 Quality Notification 576 Once this step is initiated and then concluded, be sure to set the status to Set in Process followed by setting it to Complete. The step status will turn green when the step status is set to Complete. D7 Preventive Actions In this step, we define preventive actions as tasks to prevent defects from recurring (see Figure 12.57). Choose Create followed by maintaining details of the preventive actions that are put in place to ensure that stronger quality control processes are in place. Once this step is initiated and then concluded, be sure to set the status to Set in Process fol- lowed by setting it to Complete. Figure 12.57 Preventive Action D8 Congratulate Your Team Finally, appreciate and congratulate the team for successfully implementing the entire 8D process to bring out the required improvement against nonconformance (see Figure 12.58). Once this final step is initiated and then concluded, be sure to set the sta- tus to Set in Process followed by setting it to Complete. Figure 12.58 Congratulating the Team © 577 12.7 Quality Issue Resolution Figure 12.59 shows the collapsed view of an 8D analysis via the problem-solving process for the internal problem 10000000066. The status of all eight steps is green. However, if and when any step is in process or hasn’t been started, then the system will reflect the step’s status through a different color or icon. For example, internal problem 10000000060 shows the first step is in process with a triple-forward arrows icon. Figure 12.59 Completed Status of the Internal Problem Now that we’ve covered the end-to-end business process of quality issue resolution for an internal problem through the 8D process, Figure 12.60 shows the option to not only manage the problem-solving process for internal (production/warehouse) problems but also for customers or suppliers. Figure 12.60 Customer and Supplier Problem-Solving 12 Quality Notification 578 The problem-solving options for customers or suppliers are only available in SAP S/4HANA Cloud, while our example has used on-premise SAP S/4HANA. SAP has been heavily focus- ing on the cloud-first approach to release innovations in the SAP S/4HANA Cloud offerings before these are made available for on-premises option. Figure 12.61 shows another innovation available in SAP S/4HANA Cloud that has far greater options to deep-dive into the root cause of a problem for step D4 (root causes) as compared to the on-premise SAP S/4HANA option. Here, the available options to deep-dive into root causes of a problem include the Ishikawa method, five reasons/ whys for an occurrence of a defect, and five reasons/whys for nondetection of defects are available and can be seen in the partial view of Figure 12.61. Figure 12.61 Ishikawa, 5 Whys, Occurrence, and Nondetection Process Flows Note The menu path to managing configuration changes for nonconformance management is SAP IMG  Quality Management  Nonconformance Management.

sections.title: Configuration Basics: Quality Notification
sections.en: 12.8 Configuration Basics: Quality Notification This section covers the configuration basics of quality notification.

sections.title: Overview of Notification Type
sections.en: 12.8.1 Overview of Notification Type The menu path for the overview of a notification type is SAP IMG  Quality Manage- ment  Quality Notifications  Overview of Notification Type. This is an overview of © 579 12.8 Configuration Basics: Quality Notification different notification types and their settings that are available in the system. We don’t recommend using the overview option for configuration activities because it requires an enormous amount of configuration and, as a result, entails greater like- lihood of errors occurring during the configuration process. You should use this option to review the individual configuration steps already undertaken or make any minor configuration changes.

sections.title: Notification Creation
sections.en: 12.8.2 Notification Creation In the notification creation process, you define the notification type and its content and controls, as shown in the following sections. Create Notification Type A notification type, together with its number range, is an alphanumeric identifier for different types of notifications in the system. These notification types can be a mate- rial’s defect, customer complaint, or supplier complaint. The system has three already created notification types: Q1, Q2, and Q3 (suppliers, customers, and internal quality issues, respectively). Defect notification types are defined as F1, F2, and F3 (goods issue, goods receipt, and production-related issues, respectively). The three notification origins or notification categories are also predefined in the SAP S/4HANA system. You can use these to choose proper screen controls. A complete list of notification origins is given in Table 12.3. You can customize the number ranges and screen templates for notification types to meet your organization’s needs. Finally, if a notification is outstanding and you allow this option in this configuration step, you can change the notification type from, for example, a general notification to a specific notification type. To create a notification type, follow menu path Quality Management  Quality Notifica- tions  Notification Creation  Notification Type  Define Notification Types. The initial screen that appears shows standard notification types available in the SAP system. In Notification Category Description 01 Plant maintenance 02 Quality notification 03 Service notification 04 Claim 05 General notification Table 12.3 Notification Categories 12 Quality Notification 580 addition to several other notification types used in various business functions, quality notifications Q1, Q2, and Q3 are available within the notification category Quality Noti- fication 02. Define Number Ranges We’ve talked extensively about defining and assigning number ranges to relevant objects in this book. The same basics apply for defining and assigning number ranges for notification types. To define the number ranges for a notification type, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Notification Creation  Notification Type  Define Number Ranges. Define Screen Templates In this step, you can define the screen format you want to display during notification creation of a specific notification type. To define the screen templates, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Notification Creation  Notification Types  Define Screen Templates. In the initial screen that appears, choose Define Screen Areas and Tabs. Define Screen Areas and Tabs Choose Notification Type Q2, and then choose Notification Header. Because notifica- tion type Q2 is for a complaint against a supplier, the standard SAP S/4HANA system settings have screen type header H500, which is for header quality notification. Next, for ScrnType Object (screen type object), assign the value 0510 to allow you to enter more details related to the supplier and the corresponding defective batch. An addi- tional five fields are available for you to provide additional customer-specific and ABAP-developed screens (with custom fields) for any specific or unique business needs. Next, choose Simplified View: Screen Areas on the left side, and the value in the Tab Page Allocatn (allocation) field specifies how many different screen areas you want to place on the tab page. The system provides five subscreen areas in which you can incor- porate information such as long text or reference objects (e.g., supplier number or pur- chase order number) to meet business needs. Tips and Tricks You can remove the screen options that you may not use or need. You can also modify the screen display sequence. For example, if you want Reference Documents to display first and then Reference Object, then enter value “040” in the Screen Area 2 field and value “005” in Screen Area 3. © 581 12.8 Configuration Basics: Quality Notification

sections.title: Copy Screen Areas from the Standard System
sections.en: 12.8.3 Copy Screen Areas from the Standard System Whenever you create a new notification type, it’s helpful to use the option to copy all the settings to specific database table TQSCR. For necessary configuration settings, fol- low menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Notification Creation  Notification Type  Copy Screen Areas from the Standard System. In the screen that appears, enter the newly created notification type in the relevant field, and before copying the actual notification in the database table, you can perform a test run, which can identify areas of potential conflict or problems.

sections.title: Allocate Change of Notification Type
sections.en: 12.8.4 Allocate Change of Notification Type Sometimes, it becomes necessary to change one notification type to another to reflect business requirements. You should either change or convert a general notification to a material defect notification if the defect was generated by the defective use of a mate- rial during the production process. To allocate a change of a notification type, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Notification Creation  Allocate Change of Notifi- cation Type. In the initial screen that appears, you can change notification types from the original notification type (the first column) to the target notification type (second column). Note Because this is an important control function, you can change only the notification types that you maintain in this step.

sections.title: Notification Processing
sections.en: 12.8.5 Notification Processing To control the notification process, such as notification priority response monitoring or print control, you can configure the features discussed in the following sections. Define Priorities Based on your company’s business needs, you may want to process appropriate notifi- cations according to priorities. By setting the priority, you can configure notifications to run as rush jobs or as resources become available. To define priorities, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Notification Processing  Response Control  Define Priorities. Choose Define Priorities, and then choose Priority Types. Here, you can define different priority types. Defining priority types needs to be logical, as well as relevant to the per- son or department using the priority types. 12 Quality Notification 582 Choose Priorities Notification Type and in the priority type (PrTyp column) consists of a logical grouping of all the related priority types belonging to a single group. The next column, Priority, is for the individual identification of different priorities and includes a short text column for each priority type. The Relative Start column and the number assigned will calculate the relative start date of a task in a notification. The same logic holds for the next column, Relative End. In the Choose Activity popup, choose Priority Type for Notification Type. In the change view of this screen, choose Notification Type Q2. Here, you can assign the priority type for notification type Q2. Tips and Tricks We suggest that you group the various priorities of priority type(s) into logical group- ings so that they can be more easily assigned to notification type(s) in this step. Define Response Monitoring Now that the priorities for notification types have been defined and assigned to relevant notification types, you can set up response monitoring for notification types. To set up response monitoring, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Noti- fications  Notification Processing  Response Control  Define Response Monitoring. In the screen that appears, choose Define Response Profile, and the system shows sev- eral response profiles. The default profile standard in the hierarchy is 3. A hierarchy level denotes the various escalation levels of a notification. Hierarchy level 1 indicates a high priority.

sections.title: Additional Notification Functions
sections.en: 12.8.6 Additional Notification Functions The SAP system delivers several additional notification functions. You can also add your own functions. You can define different activities using the Define Action Box and define Follow Up Actions for tasks. To set up additional notification functions, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Notification Processing  Additional Notification Functions  Define Action Box. Choose Define Functions for the Action Box, and the initial screen includes notification types. Choose Notification Type Q2 and then Notification Types. Alternatively, double- click the magnifying glass icon to view the details. The Change View Notification Types: Details screen allows you to assign a catalog profile, catalog, codes, problems, and solu- tions to Notification Type Q2. Choose Dependent Follow-Up Functions and, in in the popup, you must assign a Function Key to advance to the next screen. A function key assigned here displays a list of follow-up actions that can be performed for notification type Q2. © 583 12.8 Configuration Basics: Quality Notification Upon assigning a function key, press (Enter), and the New Entries: Overview of Added Entries screen appears. You’ll find follow-up function(s) such as Create Internal Note with Function Code 0055, which you can perform on notification type Q2 when the function key is 0035, which records details of a telephone call from a supplier or a cus- tomer. In other words, whenever a notification type Q2 has a function of logging a tele- phone call from a supplier (function key 0035), the follow-up function will be to create an internal note (function key 0055).

sections.title: Defects Recording
sections.en: 12.8.7 Defects Recording For different notification types, you can set up recording of different defects using con- firmation profiles. Confirmation profiles define the contents of the defect records. For each inspection type, you must assign appropriate notification types to properly record the defects. You can assign defects at the inspection lot level, the operation level, or the master inspection characteristic level. The system can also trigger automatic defect recording if the appropriate control indi- cator is set and the defect code is entered from catalog 9 in the catalog data. The busi- ness users set the characteristic as rejected if the results of the quality inspection reveal that tolerance levels are exceeded. Such recorded defects can generate appropriate quality notifications. You can also manually record defects at any time. To set the necessary configuration settings for defects recording and associated notifi- cation types, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Defects Recording  Define Notification Types. Choose the appropriate inspection type, such as inspection type 04. Here, you can assign notification type F3, and the system manually or automatically creates notifica- tions (depending on the other settings) whenever the business user records defects for inspection type 04. Inspection type 04 is relevant for goods receipt against production or process orders.

sections.title: Nonconformity Costs for Supplier Evaluation
sections.en: 12.8.8 Nonconformity Costs for Supplier Evaluation Chapter 19 covers the business process (and configuration details) of supplier evalua- tion that also takes quality notifications into account. In this step, you define the non- conformity costs associated with processing a quality notification for a complaint against a supplier. To define the nonconformity costs, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Information System  Define Nonconfor- mity Costs for Supplier Evaluation.

sections.title: Define Confirmation Profile
sections.en: 12.8.9 Define Confirmation Profile Confirmation profiles are used to identify required data that you want to display. To set up a confirmation profile, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifications  Defects Recording  Define Confirmation Profile. 12 Quality Notification 584 In the list of confirmation profiles that appears, you can set the various data types, such as defect type, defect location, cause, or activity, as required, optional, or none, by selecting the appropriate radio box(es). You can also create your own report format for the defect data. This provides flexibility for how you want to format the data and what data you want to include in a report. To set up a report type, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Quality Notifi- cations  Defects Recording  Define Report Type. In the popup that appears, choose Define Report Type. From the list that appears, choose or create the appropriate report type, and customize it to meet your company’s business needs. Note For the configuration or the business processes, we’ve covered quality notification integration in different chapters of this book. Briefly, quality notification integrates with the following:  Digital signature (Chapter 3, Section 3.2.3)  Reporting and evaluation (Chapter 18)  Quality control (supplier evaluation section; Chapter 19, Section 19.1)  Stability study (Chapter 15)  FMEA and control plan (Chapter 16, Section 16.2.6)

sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 12.9 Summary This chapter covered the quality notification functionality to record, monitor, and eventually resolve complaints and problems that relate to customers, suppliers, or in- house production processes. Quality notification completely integrates with several business processes, such as the Document Management System (DMS) and digital sig- nature, and offers the flexibility to perform several important business functions using an action box. Corrective and preventive action processes can be implemented by using quality notifications in QM, while further process optimization is possible by integrating corrective and preventive action with SAP Business Workflow. SAP Quality Issue Management promises to bring internal and external customer com- plaint handling to a new and much improved level. The next chapter covers engineering change management in SAP S/4HANA. ©

sections.title: Change Master
sections.en: 13.1 Change Master This section shows the configuration of the change master that begins with creating a status profile and assigning object types to it.

sections.title: Configuring a Status Profile (User Status)
sections.en: 13.1.1 Configuring a Status Profile (User Status) Apart from the checks and controls that the system offers for the change master, it’s also possible to control the flow of business transactions or incorporate greater con- trols by maintaining a status profile in the system. Note Status profiles are used throughout logistics, so you can easily and quickly integrate them with business processes. The concepts and details that we cover in this section apply to all areas in which the SAP system provides the option to maintain the user status. In engineering change management, maintaining the status profile has greater signifi- cance in the change master record. To maintain the status profile, you need to first define individual statuses within the profile, their positions with respect to each other, and the business transactions that each status can control. To create a new status profile, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Qual- ity Inspection  Status Management  Define Status Profile. For this example, in the New Entry dialog box (see Figure 13.1), set the Status Profile as “ECM_QM00”, enter a short Text description, define the Maintenance Language as English (EN), and choose Con- tinue to go to the Change Status Profile: User Status screen shown in Figure 13.2. Figure 13.1 Initial Screen for Status Profile In Figure 13.2, enter “1” for the Status Number, followed by a Status code of “CHEK” and a short text. In addition, select the Init. status indicator to denote that this should always be the initial status of the business function. Define the lowest and the highest statuses for this status—that is, whether a lower status can be changed back to a higher status. Repeat the same steps for the next status, which is APPR. © 587 13.1 Change Master Figure 13.2 Status Profile for User Status Choose Object Types, located at the top of the screen, to go to the Change Status Profile: Allowed Object Types screen shown in Figure 13.3. Figure 13.3 Allowed Object Types for User Status Profiles Figure 13.3 contains the list of all the standard object types available in the system from which you can select to trigger the status profile for the relevant business functions. Because you’re creating the status profile specifically for engineering change manage- ment in this example, select the following three object types:  ECM Context  ECM change master record  ECM change objects 13 Engineering Change Management 588 Note If you integrate the status profile (user status) into other areas of the SAP S/4HANA system, then you also need to select the relevant object types at this stage. Choose Back to go back to the Change Status Profile: User Status screen. Select the first status, CHEK, and choose Detail. This leads to the Transaction Control screen shown in Figure 13.4. Figure 13.4 Detailed View of Status Profiles Choose New, and, for the CHEK status, select the Convert ECR radio button in the Allowed column to allow the business user to convert the engineering change record into an engi- neering change object when the user status is set to CHEK. The other options available for user status for a specific transaction and their influence are listed here:  No influence  Warning  Forbidd. For the same status, you can set the next action of a business transaction. These are shown in the last two columns with the No action and Set radio buttons (see Figure 13.5). For this example, repeat the same step with status APPR, but also select the Allowed radio button and the Set radio button. Save the settings. © 589 13.1 Change Master Figure 13.5 Transaction Control for Status APPR

sections.title: Maintain the Profile
sections.en: 13.1.2 Maintain the Profile Maintaining the system profile for engineering change management enables the user to maintain default values, which saves time and effort by reducing redundant entries. To maintain the profile, follow menu path SAP IMG  Cross-Application Components  Engineering Change Management  Maintain Profile. Figure 13.6 Maintaining the Profile 13 Engineering Change Management 590 It’s important to note that you can set the user status profile here—for example, set- ting ECM_QM00 (created earlier) in the status profile (see Figure 13.6). Choose Object type profile (overview) at the left of the screen, and the screen in Figure 13.7 appears. In Figure 13.7, assign and select the previously created status profile ECM_QM01, and then choose Object type profile (detail). The screen in Figure 13.8 appears. Figure 13.8 offers the control of different object types, such as an inspection plan or a material bill of materials (BOM) to which the configured status profile can be assigned. During master data changes such as changes to an inspection plan or material BOM, the system will offer relevant objects types for selection to which the status profile will already be assigned. Be sure to deselect the Lock checkbox to ensure that you’re able to maintain entries while creating a change master record. Figure 13.7 Object Type Profile Figure 13.8 Object Types © 591 13.1 Change Master Table 13.1 provides a selected list of object types you can automate in the engineering change management change master record. It also shows that you can integrate engi- neering change management with the master data of QM, production planning (PP), plant maintenance (PM), and Document Management System (DMS) in SAP S/4HANA. Let’s now turn to the business processes of the change master and engineering change request creation.

sections.title: Change Master Creation
sections.en: 13.1.3 Change Master Creation To create the change master, follow menu path Cross-Application Components  Engi- neering Change Management  Change Number  Create, or use Transaction CC01. In this initial screen (see Figure 13.9), select the Change Package and Without Release Key radio buttons, and press (Enter), which leads to the Create Change Master: Change Header screen (see Figure 13.10). Object Type Object Type Description 02 Material BOM 03 Equipment BOM 05 Functional location BOM 06 Standard BOM 07 Order BOM 12 Routing 13 Reference operation set 21 Inspection plan 24 Master recipe 25 Rate routing 26 Reference rate routing 27 Functional location task list 31 Document 41 Material 51 Characteristic 52 Characteristics of class 53 Classification Table 13.1 Selected Standard Object Types Available in SAP S/4HANA 13 Engineering Change Management 592 Figure 13.9 Create Change Master Figure 13.10 Create Change Master: Header Data Note You can enter the profile in the Control area of the screen shown in Figure 13.9 so that the system automatically brings up preselected and predefined values. To maintain the system profile, refer to Section 13.1.2. © 593 13.1 Change Master In the header data of the change master, enter a short text, and enter “01/01/2024” in the Valid From field of the change master. You can also enter a short text in the Reason for Change field. As the initial status of a change master was configured to have the CHEK status, the system automatically assigns it here. It’s important to assign a change number status (Change no. status field) to the change master to denote whether it’s active or inactive. For this example, enter “1” to denote that it’s active. Choose the Object Types button to open the screen shown in Figure 13.11, which lists all the objects to which the change master can apply. For this example, select the Actv. checkbox for the Inspection Plan object to denote that you’re only going to manage changes in the inspection plan (task list) by the change master. Figure 13.11 Object Types in Change Master Note You generally come across the term task list in several SAP areas. While a task list denotes sequence of operations or steps involved, it’s the task list type that specifically identifies where a particular task list is in use. For example, task list type Q denotes an inspection plan that is used in QM, and other task list types are specific to routing, rate routing, and master recipe. 13 Engineering Change Management 594 Next, choose Objects, and then set the task list (TLstTy) as Q (for inspection plan), the Group as 1, and the Description as “Add a new master inspection characteristic”. A group is a unique identification of an individual task list (see Figure 13.11). Next, select Objects in the screen in Figure 13.11, and then in Figure 13.12, maintain the object level details, such as a material and its plant, which in this example are FG129 and 1710, respectively. Tips and Tricks Choose the Lock checkbox in Figure 13.11 only if you don’t want a user to make any changes to an object, such as an inspection plan or a routing. Figure 13.12 Object Type and Object in Change Master Save the entry, and the system internally generates a change master number, which for this example is 500000000010 (see Figure 13.13). Figure 13.13 Change Master © 595 13.1 Change Master

sections.title: Changes in Inspection Plan with a Change Number
sections.en: 13.1.4 Changes in Inspection Plan with a Change Number With the change master for the inspection plan created in the system, let’s now make actual changes in the inspection plan with reference to the change master. To change the task list (inspection plan), use Transaction QP02 (see Figure 13.14). Figure 13.14 Initial Screen of Inspection Plan with Change Number Enter the Material as “FG129”, Plant as “1710”, and Group as “1”. Notice that this is the same group 1 that you entered in the last step shown in Figure 13.12. In addition, enter the Change Number as “500000000010” and the valid-from date (Key Date) as “03/19/ 2024”, and then choose the Header button. The system overwrites the date (03/19/ 2024) because it automatically refers to the date maintained in the change master (which is 01/01/2024). Refer to Figure 13.10 again. Note It’s important to ensure that the header of the inspection plan has the change rule set as 1 for the change number. As we’re now making changes to the inspection plan with reference to the change num- ber, the system will record or update any changes made, and the information will be available with reference to the change number in the engineering change management information system. Choose the Operations button shown in Figure 13.15, and then select line item 0010 with Work Center QMLABS, shown in Figure 13.16. 13 Engineering Change Management 596 Figure 13.15 Header Details of the Inspection Plan Figure 13.16 Operation Overview of the Inspection Plan Next, choose More  Inspection Characteristics. In the screen shown in Figure 13.17, enter a new master inspection characteristic, “PURITY”, and save the entries. The sys- tem will automatically bring up the default values that were previously assigned to this master inspection characteristic at the time of its creation. With all these changes made to the inspection plan with reference to change number 500000000010, let’s now evaluate the changes in the engineering change manage- ment information system. © 597 13.1 Change Master Figure 13.17 Operation Details

sections.title: Engineering Change Management Information System
sections.en: 13.1.5 Engineering Change Management Information System Leveraging the strength of the information system in the SAP S/4HANA system, engi- neering change management also has its own set of reports and its own information system for users to get relevant, comprehensive information from based on user- defined criteria. Figure 13.18 Engineering Change Management Information System 13 Engineering Change Management 598 To view changes made to the inspection plan with reference to the change number, fol- low menu path Cross-Application Components  Engineering Change Management  Reporting  Information System or use Transaction CC07. Figure 13.18 shows the initial screen for the engineering change management information system. Many options and relevant parameters are available for use so that when the report executes, the sys- tem displays only the relevant results. In this screen, enter only the Change Number, “500000000010”, and then choose the Execute button (not shown). In the screen that appears (see Figure 13.19), double-click change number 500000000010 under Product Structure to see a summary of all the important information with refer- ence to the change number on the right side of the screen. For this example, we drill down into the comprehensive details available on the left side of the screen to show you the system structure and the entire task list (inspection plan). Figure 13.19 Engineering Change Management Information System The following section discusses the change record in SAP S/4HANA. © 599

sections.title: Change Record
sections.en: 13.2 Change Record 13.2 Change Record Engineering change management with change records offers the flexibility to support the management of engineering changes. It can handle several types of objects, such as materials, material BOMs, and documents (from DMS) that are affected by the intended changes. The engineering record keeps all information in one place. Status manage- ment controls the entire progress of change, and the change process is also supported by the workflow capabilities. Communication with SAP CoPilot during the change pro- cess allows effective communication with all involved parties. Some of the key process steps covered by change records are as follows:  Determine responsibility  Create change record  Start workflow  Approve change request (optional)  Rework request  Assign design document  Assign material, BOM, and BOM items  Approve or reject change request  Modify validity date in the change master  Perform design changes  Perform material changes  Perform BOM or BOM item changes We’ll now create a change record with an example that will also simultaneously create a change master (as already discussed in the previous section). The flexibility to create a change master when a change record is created is controlled via configuration. Note The change record configuration can be found via menu path SAP IMG  Logistics – General  Product Lifecycle Management (PLM)  Change Records.

sections.title: Manage Engineering Changes
sections.en: 13.2.1 Manage Engineering Changes Figure 13.20 shows the Manage Engineering Changes app, which is accessed from the Engineering Cockpit app. Once in the Engineering Cockpit app (shown later in Figure 13.28), choose Change Record. To create a new change record, choose Create Change Record, and then choose Change Record in S/4HANA from the dropdown; this will bring up Figure 13.21. As already noted, the different types of change records can be configured to meet a company’s business needs. Figure 13.20 shows four such change record types. 13 Engineering Change Management 600 Figure 13.20 Manage Engineering Changes Figure 13.21 shows part of the detail screen used to maintain more information of a change record. Scroll down or choose from one of the available tabs, and the screen in Figure 13.22 appears. Figure 13.21 Header Details of a Change Record © 601 13.2 Change Record Figure 13.22 Relevance Selection in a Change Record Figure 13.22 shows the relevance of a change record and if the same triggers any follow- on action or activity, such as creating a new version of a change record. Choose Change (CNG) from the dropdown under the Relevance field, followed by choosing the forward arrow (>), and the screen in Figure 13.23 appears. Figure 13.23 shows the item details of a change record in which the engineering BOM of material MZ-FG-C900 in plant 1710 with BOM usage 1 (production) and its BOM version 1 is subject to a change record. Save the change record, and the change number shown in Figure 13.24 will appear. Figure 13.23 Maintaining Engineering BOM Details in a Change Record Figure 13.24 shows change record 100000000000000046, consisting of header and item details. From the dropdown on the right side of the screen, first choose Accept Change Request (refer to Figure 13.23), which will change the status of this change 13 Engineering Change Management 602 record. Next, choose Send Change Request for Approval, and save. Doing so will accord- ingly update the status of the change record. Once the necessary and requested changes to a change record are ensured, the status can be changed again as shown later in Figure 13.26. Figure 13.24 Change Status in a Change Record Figure 13.25 shows the options for a change manager to either accept, approve, or reject the change request. Further, you can even merge or split different change records to meet any specific business needs. The relevant options to merge or split change records are located on the top-right side of the screen. Figure 13.25 Decisions for a Change Request Figure 13.26 shows the option to choose Complete Change so that no further changes to the change record can be made. Figure 13.26 Change Record © 603 13.2 Change Record

sections.title: Manage Change Records
sections.en: 13.2.2 Manage Change Records Figure 13.27 shows the Manage Change Records app with the change record type Change Record in S/4HANA (S04) and the change record number 100000000000000046. Figure 13.27 Manage Change Record

sections.title: Engineering Cockpit
sections.en: 13.2.3 Engineering Cockpit Figure 13.28 shows the Engineering Cockpit app with various cards that can be clicked individually to navigate to view the details. This overview page helps development man- agers review the engineering execution status of various change records and take actions quickly. Some of the other key features of the Engineering Cockpit are as follows:  View urgent engineering changes by expected completion date.  See the lifecycle status of change records in a specific time scope (last four weeks, months, or quarters).  Get the engineering progress in a specific time scope (last four weeks, months, or quarters) via a line chart.  View the upcoming effective changes.  Provide quick links to the Manage Engineering Changes, My Inbox, and Manage Documents apps. In the following section, we’ll discuss the Engineering Record app in SAP S/4HANA. 13 Engineering Change Management 604 Figure 13.28 Engineering Cockpit

sections.title: Engineering Record
sections.en: 13.3 Engineering Record The Engineering Record app allows the BOM engineer to manage engineering changes. For example, the BOM engineer can use this app to monitor change progress on a reg- ular basis and create new changes in response to certain events. Some of the key fea- tures of this app are as follows:  Create engineering records  View engineering records  Search engineering records  Filter displayed results Note The Engineering Record app configuration can be found via menu path SAP IMG  Logistics – General  Product Lifecycle Management (PLM)  PLM Web User Interface  Objects in PLM Web UI  Engineering Record  Make Settings for Engineering Records. We’ll show with an example how to create an engineering record, including the approval routes that can be interactively defined and how an engineering record auto- matically creates a change record too. Access the screen in Figure 13.29 via the Manage Engineering Record app. On the initial screen, choose the relevant Engineering Record Type from the dropdown, along with maintaining other details such as the Release Coordinator and Target Run-In Date, which is the date by which the engineering record must be approved. © 605 13.3 Engineering Record Figure 13.29 Engineering Record: Initial Screen Figure 13.30 shows the detailed view of an engineering record. The right side of the screen shows the Engineering Record Status dropdown that includes the various sta- tuses for an engineering record. The option is available to maintain a business partner in SAP S/4HANA along with a customer reference. A business user can maintain infor- mation not just in the main tabs located in the lower half of the screen but also in the subtabs available within a main tab, such as Items. In the Material BOM tab, maintain the Material “MZ-FG-C900” for Plant “1710” with BOM Usage “1” and Alternative “1”. Other subtabs are also available to maintain related information. Subtabs that appear here are directly controlled via configuration. Choose the Process Route tab, and the screen in Figure 13.31 appears. Figure 13.30 Material BOM Assignment in the Engineering Record 13 Engineering Change Management 606 In Figure 13.31, it’s possible to define parallel and/or sequential tasks so that the work- flow triggers the same for the engineering record. To add a sequential task, choose Add Sequential Task; the screen in Figure 13.32 appears. Figure 13.31 Creating an Engineering Record In Figure 13.32, you can maintain the details of the sequential task and the activity asso- ciated with a task. Options to set a task priority and to set a timeline or a deadline are also available. Figure 13.32 Adding a Sequential Task to a Process Route © 607 13.3 Engineering Record Figure 13.33 shows the parallel task with the assigned Activity as Final Signature; the Task Priority is defined as 1 Highest - Express. Figure 13.33 Adding Parallel Tasks to a Process Route Figure 13.34 shows the summarized view of the process tasks within a process route. Figure 13.34 Process Route In Figure 13.35, set the Engineering Record Status located on the top-right side as 10- Release Inquiry (Initial) and save; the message shown in Figure 13.36 appears. Figure 13.35 Changing the Status of an Engineering Record 13 Engineering Change Management 608 Figure 13.36 shows that the system has created engineering record 2 and has also simul- taneously created an associated change number, 500000000015. Recall from the pre- vious discussion that it’s possible for the system to simultaneously and automatically create a change number as soon as an engineering record is created. Figure 13.36 Message on Creating an Engineering Record Figure 13.37 shows engineering record number 2 and the associated lead change num- ber 500000000015. Figure 13.37 Change Number Assigned to an Engineering Record Figure 13.38 is accessed using Transaction CS02 to change material BOM MZ-FG-C900 in plant 1710. Notice the Change No., 500000000015, which will record any changes made to the material BOM. After changes to the material BOM are complete, Figure 13.39 shows engineering record 2, in which the business user can set subsequent statuses, such as releasing the order or if the release request is rejected. Figure 13.40 shows that when engineering record 2 has attained the status Release Completed, the system no longer allows any further changes to the engineering record. This control function ensures that an engineering record is locked from any further changes. © 609 13.3 Engineering Record Figure 13.38 Material BOM with Change Number Figure 13.39 Status Change of an Engineering Record Figure 13.40 BOM Details in an Engineering Record 13 Engineering Change Management 610 Figure 13.41 and Figure 13.42 are accessed via the Manage Engineering Records app. Figure 13.42 is accessed by scrolling to the right side of Figure 13.41. Notice that engineering record 2 has the associated change number 500000000015. If a change number is already in use in any of the master data objects, then this will be reflected in the In Use column, as shown for change master 500000000015. Figure 13.41 Manage Engineering Records App Figure 13.42 Manage Change Masters App The next section discusses the management of changes process in SAP S/4HANA sys- tem. © 611

sections.title: Management of Changes
sections.en: 13.4 Management of Changes 13.4 Management of Changes Management of changes is a highly flexible and fully auditable process in SAP S/4HANA for requesting, monitoring, and implementing changes. For example, a change request can introduce a new chemical in the production process or modify operating condi- tions of a piece of equipment. This change management tool can be used to do the fol- lowing:  Automate identification of risk experts, approvers, and subject-matter experts.  Enable employees and contractors to request changes easily.  Streamline the change process and drive forward consistency and standardization.  Provide workflow and status management to ensure task completion. A change request is a requirement for an adjustment to be made within a company, a plant, or a process. When creating a change request, you first select the type of changes involved. This change request type defines the details of a change request to be queried—for example, related objects, activities, and questionnaires. A change request can be used by anyone in the company or in the plant to report an incident or a need for any improvement. Figure 13.43 Change Request Types in the Configuration Menu Path 13 Engineering Change Management 612 The lifecycle of a change request starts as soon as the change request is created. It’s based on the change request’s status network. This lifecycle can be managed by setting the appropriate status. Further, you can also automate status changes so that the status of the change request changes automatically when a certain activity has reached a cer- tain status. To configure a new change request type in SAP S/4HANA, follow menu path SAP IMG  Cross-Application Components  Management of Change. Figure 13.43 shows the configuration node for Management of Change. As you can see, several of these areas were already discussed in various sections and chapters of this book. For example, Chapter 2 discussed catalogs and code groups, Chapter 3 discussed digital signatures, and Section 13.1.1 discussed status profile maintenance (user status); hence, these and associated topics aren’t repeated here. Choose Define Change Request Types, shown in Figure 13.43, and the screen in Figure 13.44 appears. Figure 13.44 Change Request Type Figure 13.44 shows a new change request type (CR Type) MOC with the description MOC Change Request. Later, you’ll see that the system prompts the user to choose the change request’s description when creating a new change request. Other details, such as first creating and then assigning number range intervals (see Figure 13.43 again) for a change request, as well as for activities, are shown. The left side offers more options to customize each change request type, such as assigning the previously defined digital signature and automating the status change when a specific status of a change request has been reached. Access the screen shown in Figure 13.45 via the Create Change Request app. As you can see, the system offers the option to choose a change request’s description and not the change request type. Choose MOC Change Request, and the screen in Figure 13.46 appears. © 613 13.4 Management of Changes Figure 13.46 shows the partial display of the change request in which relevant details such as the object type, object reference, and date can be maintained. Notice that the status of the change request here is In Preparation. Figure 13.45 Create Change Request Figure 13.46 Object Information and Dates in Change Request It’s important to understand how the predecessor-successor relationship for a status network works in a change request. Table 13.2 shows that when a change request’s status is In Preparation, the next and the only available status is Submitted. When a change request is submitted, not only is the change request’s status automatically updated, but with a Submitted status, the next four (successor) statuses become available: Awaiting, Incomplete, Rejected, Not Applicable, and On Hold. As soon as the change request attains one of these five statuses, the system makes available the corresponding successors or next statuses, as shown in the Current Status column in Table 13.2. 13 Engineering Change Management 614 Current Status Description Possible Actions to Trigger Status Change New Status In Preparation Draft version is being created by a reporter. Here, it’s also possible to categorize the impact that a product or the process will have if the suggested change isn’t implemented. Scroll down in the screen in Figure 13.47, and the screen in Figure 13.48 appears. Figure 13.47 Change Definition in Change Request Figure 13.48 shows the Object Type Material and the associated Object (material num- ber in this case) that can be selected from the dropdown. Although this example only shows material as an option type to choose from, there are several other object types that can be made available in the dropdown and via the configuration option (refer to Figure 13.44). In the lower half of the screen, the Attachments and Links option enables On Hold The change process is stopped—for example, due to a missing budget—but it’s planned to recommence at a later point in time. Remove Hold Status before Set- ting Hold Not Applicable The requested change isn’t suitable for an official change process. Scroll down, and the screen in Figure 13.49 will appear. Figure 13.48 Related Objects in a Change Request Figure 13.49 shows the people or the stakeholders involved in enabling a change request; they can be reviewers, approvers, or business analysts. It’s important to note that the business partners must be previously created and can then be assigned here. If the digital signature is configured and assigned to a change request, then the option to digitally sign it is also available here. A digital signature will trigger when a change request has attained a specific status in which the stakeholder must digitally sign the change request to confirm the new status. Figure 13.49 People Involved and Digital Signature in a Change Request Save the change request by choosing Save and Submit located at the bottom-right side of the screen, and the screen in Figure 13.50 appears. A change request can also be saved as a draft and can be submitted later. Figure 13.50 shows the header of the change request, which now has the change request number 1000000001. Figure 13.51 shows the activities associated with this change request; in this example, the change request needs to be approved. Notice that though the change request num- ber is 1000000001, the activity number is 700000002. Each change number can have © 617 13.4 Management of Changes multiple activities, and every activity is uniquely identified by its own number. To make changes to a change number, choose Edit located at the top-left side of Figure 13.50. Figure 13.50 Change Request 1000000001 with In Preparation Status Figure 13.51 Activities in a Change Request Access Figure 13.52 via the Manage Change Request app, and you’ll see that the status of change request 1000000001 is Submitted. Other available statuses are shown via the dropdown, thus making it easier for the relevant stakeholders to quickly attend to change requests that need any subsequent action. Figure 13.52 Manage Change Requests Access the screen shown in Figure 13.53 via the Manage Change Activities app to set var- ious available filters so that the app only displays the relevant information, as well as 13 Engineering Change Management 618 display additional columns. You can also navigate to the detailed screen of an individ- ual activity of a change request. Figure 13.53 Manage Change Activities Figure 13.54 shows the Change Requests Dashboard app that provides complete and comprehensive visibility into all the change requests made so far and their statuses. If needed, users can navigate to the detailed screen by choosing the forward arrow located at the far-right side of the screen. The app shows a combination of tabular and graphical combinations for easier comprehension. Figure 13.54 Change Request Dashboard © 619

sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 13.5 Summary Note Visit http://s-prs.co/v492401 to learn more about management of changes in SAP S/4HANA. Be sure to choose the relevant or correct SAP S/4HANA version so that SAP Help brings up the required information. 13.5 Summary This chapter covered the necessary configuration needed for successfully integrating engineering change management with business processes. The user status (status profile) has greater relevance in the change master. The engineering change manage- ment information system provides in-depth and comprehensive details of all the changes made and enables the user to select status-based information for further necessary action. Newer master data change management tools to manage changes in SAP S/4HANA are change record, engineering record, and management of changes. The next chapter covers audit management in SAP S/4HANA. ©

sections.title: Overview
sections.en: 14.1 Overview Figure 14.1 shows an overview of the steps involved in audit management. Figure 14.1 Audit Management Set up audits within audit plan Create or assign question list to audit Print audit with question list Perform actual/ physical audit Enter info on audit’s questions Valuate and complete audit Set up audit plan Enter corrective/ preventive action for failed questions 14 Audit Management 622 During the audit planning stage, you prepare the necessary question lists and audit cri- teria, depending on the relevant standards, regulations, or rules of the auditable area. You can set up an audit plan and define the periodic schedule, taking into consider- ation the scope, audit object, and dates of the audits. When the audit is part of a pro- gram, you need to set up the audit plan and any relevant audit subplans. The subplans should contain information about the plan, a general description, and a validity period. This is often the case for obligatory audits, in which case, we recommend that you use the audit program. The audit program allows you to plan the type, scope, and fre- quency of audits, as well as the resource requirements. You can create an audit pro- gram by hierarchically structuring audit plans (Figure 14.1 1), which also allows you to combine certain types of audits. From a business perspective, it makes sense to group together an environment audit and health and safety audit, for example. During an actual audit, you collect evidence and record the findings. Prepare or set up the individual audits 2 by determining the question lists 3, identifying the partners involved, and preparing the required documents. This step involves the following actions: releasing the audit in the system, inviting the participants, providing the doc- uments, and examining the audit object with regard to the criteria, or performing interviews with the relevant stakeholders. Although audit management is designed for online, paperless applications, SAP sup- ports exporting and importing audit data and audit question lists 4 to allow for offline and mobile auditing through a standard XML interface. The XML file can then be trans- ferred to a Microsoft Excel file and loaded onto the auditor’s laptop so that the auditor can perform the actual audit 5 on this data. The auditor can then upload the file via the standard XML interface into audit management, where the auditor can process the remaining steps or complete the audit process. Based on the evidence entered in the previous step 6, the system valuates the ques- tions based on the question configuration settings (set up to meet your company’s business rules), so the system rates and automatically grades an audit object. Because you’re valuating the audit object, this stage is sometimes referred to as a grade audit or a grade object. The overall assessment and grading for the audit object is determined on the basis of the valuations of all items that have actually been assessed. To consoli- date the valuations across several hierarchy levels of the question list, the system uses the degrees of fulfillment or deviation from each hierarchy level for calculation in the standard SAP S/4HANA system. The valuation on the supreme hierarchy level is then used to grade the audit object. In the rating profile, you determine the degrees of fulfillment that must be achieved for separate audit objects. In this step, you create an audit report, which contains all important administrative data related to the audit, including comments, results, and the corrective/preventive actions taken 7. The audit report is an official document. © 623

sections.title: Setting Up Audit Objects
sections.en: 14.2 Setting Up Audit Objects After the assessment, you can create a preliminary audit report, which you can then use to discuss the findings, corrective actions, and overall results of the audit. The audit can then be signed (physically or using a digital signature), created, and distributed. The system represents the signature by the status of the audit. If the signature itself must be documented and verified, you can scan the signed report into the system and attach it to the audit 8. During an audit, if the auditors detect that there are inadmissible deviations, dangers, or room for improvement, they can note their findings and make recommendations, determine the need for a subsequent audit, or create corrective or preventive actions for the relevant items of the audit question list. The last step of audit management focuses on monitoring the outstanding actions and finalizing the audit report. Note We recommend that you also read Chapter 16 on failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), which highly overlaps with the functionality and basics of audit management. In fact, FMEA is a specialized form of audit that finds greater application in the auto- motive industry. 14.2 Setting Up Audit Objects The following audit objects are used within audit management:  Audit plan  Audit  Question list  Question

sections.title: Set Up the Audit Plan
sections.en: 14.2.1 Set Up the Audit Plan An audit plan is used to keep an overview of the audits that the company undertakes and have them organized in a logical way. An audit plan is also known as an audit pro- gram. In the audit plan, you define the schema in the form of an annual schedule by taking into consideration the scope, object, and date of the audits. An audit plan can contain several subordinate audit plans and links to audits. You can access the audit management work area from Transaction PLMD_Audit or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Audit Management  Audit Management. The resulting screen, shown in Figure 14.2, divides the entire audit management work area into three distinct sections. In the top-left work area (known as the structure tree), the system provides options to create new objects, such as an audit plan, audit, or 14 Audit Management 624 question list. You can also copy one audit item to another, delete an item within audit management, or even look up specific information. All of these options are available via the New icon’s dropdown list available at the top-left side of Figure 14.2. Figure 14.2 Audit Management Workbench The right side of the screen (known as the detail screen) is blank unless you’re already working on a specific audit object. The lower-left side (known as the worklist/template area) shows the audits or other objects that you’ve worked on in the recent past and is available in the work area’s history. To make more space in the work area, you can hide the details shown on the lower-left side of the screen by choosing Close (the blue cross—hidden behind the dropdown). Choose the New icon in Figure 14.2 to create a new audit plan, question list, or audit either from scratch or using a template. Choose Audit Plan from the dropdown list, and the system brings up the screen shown in Figure 14.3. Here, you see the basic data view of an audit plan. On the right side of the screen, enter “NSA” in the Audit Plan field (for the rest of this chapter, we’ll be using the audit plan NSA as an example to denote new suppliers’ audits), and enter its description. Notice the additional icons next to the Audit Plan field that enable you to add additional notes, attachments, or even web links for reference and records purposes. The option to attach documents or notes is also generally available while you’re creating all items of audit management. Similarly, you can keep an eye on the alerts and messages that are available at the top-right side. © 625 14.2 Setting Up Audit Objects Figure 14.3 Audit Plan Double-click the message icon, and details of the message appear at the bottom of the same screen. We suggest that you take time out to explore the tools and menus. Enter the valid from and valid to dates of your audit plan. At this time, the system status of the audit plan is Being Created. You need to release the audit plan before you can actu- ally begin working with it. In the Texts tab, you can incorporate more details about the audit plan, including add- ing a description and notes. You can even upload (and download) the content from some other data source, such as another drive on your laptop, and incorporate it in either the description or note areas of the audit plan. This is possible when you choose the relevant upload or download options. Note The option to enter various types of texts is generally available in the Texts tab of all items of audit management. Choose the Contact Person tab in Figure 14.3, and the system brings up the screen shown in Figure 14.4 1. Here, you enter the roles and names of the people who will be part of the audit plan team. You can assign responsibilities to the relevant persons, and then in all subsequent status updates or reporting, information on participants helps in finding whose tasks are pending or overdue, or even which resource/participant is assigned to what task(s). 14 Audit Management 626 Tips and Tricks Use Transaction BP to create or amend business partners (team members) who will be part of the audit management initiative. Choose the Status tab 2. Here, the current status of the audit plan is still in the creation phase. Save your audit plan. The next step is to create an audit. Figure 14.4 Contact Person and Status in Audit Plan

sections.title: Set Up Audit
sections.en: 14.2.2 Set Up Audit The audit (also known as an audit plan within ISO 19011, whereas an audit plan is known as an audit program) describes the audit type and audit triggers, as well as the audit object. The definition of audit objects makes it possible to analyze similar audits to determine best practices or trends. The structure of an audit consists of the following elements: © 627 14.2 Setting Up Audit Objects  Audit plan This is an optional element for reoccurring audits.  Audit This is the object being audited, such as the product or process, audit team, audit type and cause, deadlines, texts, valuation rule, result, or status.  Audit question list The question and/or question list gets assigned to the audit. As soon as you use a question list or create a question list or additional questions, these all are specific to the audit and contain both the question list header and items.  Corrective/preventive actions This is related to audit questions, which contain follow-up actions such as an addi- tional audit, or preventive, corrective, or improvement actions. To set up an audit, right-click audit plan NSA so that the system brings up the option to create an audit (see Figure 14.5). Choose Create and then choose Audit 1. Enter the name of the audit, together with its short description. The system prompts you to select the Audit Type, which can be a system, product, or process audit type available according to your configured objects. Refer to Section 14.6.2 on configuration objects for audit types. Figure 14.5 Audit Setup 14 Audit Management 628 Choose 51 System Audit at Vendor’s Site as the Audit Type 2, and then choose 60 Change of Manufacturing Process as the Audit Trigger. Enter Business Partner “9980000210” and QM System “ISO_9001”. Then, enter the planned start and end dates of the audit in the lower half of the screen. You can update the actual start and end dates of your audit in the bottom half of the screen when you actually start and then complete the audit. Choose the Texts tab in 2 so that you can incorporate more details about the audit, including adding its detailed description and notes. Choose the Result tab in Figure 14.6, and notice that because you’re creating a new audit, the Audit Result area reflects that the system hasn’t assessed the audit yet, nor the audit’s degree of fulfillment, so the fields are all blank. Later, you’ll see how the sys- tem automatically fills up these fields after it calculates the audit results. In the lower half of the screen (the Valuation Specifications area), select the procedure that you want to use as the valuation specification for the audit. For this example, set the valuation Procedure to Valuation Acc. to Fulfillment (Absol., Minimum Result Determines. Figure 14.6 Valuation Specification of Audit Before the system calculates the audit results, it asks the business process owner to assign a rating profile. A rating profile refers to the predefined segregation to valuate whether the audit results should valuate the supplier as, for example, low risk, high risk, or no risk at all. In addition, it’s important to note that you have to define the minimum result that the audit must achieve as 90.0. In other words, it acts a bench- mark to compare actual audit findings with minimum results and enables the system © 629 14.2 Setting Up Audit Objects to conduct Overall Assest. (assessment) to declare findings from the audit as a success or failure. Save your entries. The next step is to create an audit question list or questions.

sections.title: Set Up the Question List/Questions
sections.en: 14.2.3 Set Up the Question List/Questions A question list (also referred to as audit criteria) is usually required to execute an audit, and it stores the criteria against which the audit objects are assessed. Question lists contain the expertise of the auditor regarding the audit area. A question list can be cre- ated as an independent master data object with the purpose of reusing its contents. After you create an audit, you can assign this question list into the audit, which makes it part of the audit. This, however, is optional; you can also create the question list spe- cifically for a particular audit. In Figure 14.7, choose Audit on the left side of the screen. The system brings up the option to create an audit question list/question. Choose Audit Question List/Question 1, and a popup appears. The Hierarchy Prof. (profile) field 2 controls different levels of audit question lists or questions. For example, a question list or a question may have further parts or elements that form its overall structure. With hierarchy control, you can control this, as well as which question, part, or element the system should valuate during an audit valuation. Choose Question; Figure 14.8 shows the valuation details of the question. Figure 14.7 Question List 14 Audit Management 630 Figure 14.8 shows View Selection, which offers the option to maintain details of the question, whereas the Valuation view is the option that you use in the business process of audit management. At this time, you’re maintaining the setup for audit manage- ment, so maintain the question’s details, such as texts and valuation specifications. Choose Valuations Specs to go to the screen in Figure 14.9. Figure 14.8 Basic Data of the Question List Figure 14.9 1 consists of the calculation procedure, as well as the valuation of the ques- tion that you saw while creating the audit. Here, again, the Minimum Result for this question should be 90.0. You can control the weighting that this question can have. For example, a weighting of 2 enables the system to give twice the weight or importance to this question during audit calculation (valuation). Valuation Profile controls whether you can enter the result of the question as a percentage, quantity, or code (also contains either a percentage or valuation on a scale of 1 to 100). A ValuatnProposal (valuation pro- posal) of 90.0 automatically brings this value up for the business user as a default value, which may deviate from the actual audit finding/assessment of this question. Figure 14.9 also shows the dropdown options available for Procedures 2 and ValuatnProfile 3. Note The configuration details of procedures and the valuation profile are explained in Chapter 16. Tips and Tricks If you have a business need to print the audit question list at the time of conducting an actual or physical audit, then while in the audit, choose Print Preview. The system shows the print preview of the entire audit and enables you to print it directly or save it as a PDF file that you can print later. Refer to Figure 14.5 1 to check out the Print Pre- view option available for an audit. © 631

sections.title: Business Processes
sections.en: 14.3 Business Processes You can also create a question list in advance and then assign it when the actual audit is conducted so that the latest and most updated question list applies to the audit. The option to create a question list is available when you first create an audit plan or an audit. To assign an already-created question list to an audit, refer to Figure 14.7 1 and choose Assign Question List. Figure 14.9 Valuation Specifications for Question 14.3 Business Processes Audit management is suitable for a variety of audit usages, and you can easily combine audits where this is possible. The following are some examples in which you can use audit management: 14 Audit Management 632  ISO 9000 (quality management) is a group of standards developed by the Interna- tional Organization for Standardization (ISO), which provides guidance and tools for companies and organizations that want to ensure their products and services con- sistently meet customer requirements and quality consistently improves. It includes audit management, in which organizations must perform internal audits to check how its QM system is working. Audits can be related to systems, processes, or products, as well as FMEA.  Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) is a production and testing practice that helps to ensure a quality product. Many countries have legislations covering GMP proce- dures and guidelines specifically for pharmaceutical and medical device companies to safeguard the health of the patient, as well as produce good quality medicine, medical devices, or active pharmaceutical products.  ISO 14000 (environmental management) is another group of standards from ISO that provides practical tools for companies and organizations looking to identify and control their environmental impact and constantly improve their environmen- tal performance.  ISO 19000 (safety and security management) is a group of standards for geographic information, including concepts, principles of quality, quality assessment, specifica- tions, and metadata standards. ISO 19011 provides guidance on auditing manage- ment systems, the principles of auditing, management of an audit program, and the evaluation of competence of the individuals involved in the audit process. Example Textile, garments, and home furnishing buyers (e.g., Walmart, JCPenney, and the Gap) often require manufacturers to undergo rigorous rounds of multiple audits to ensure the safety and security of textile workers and to meet fire and safety hazard prevention requirements. These buyer-specific audits can be managed in audit management. The business processes in audit management begin with releasing the audit plan for all stakeholders to sign their consent to all elements of the audit plan. This is followed by releasing individual audits as and when they near. On releasing the audit, the auditor can actually start attending to each audit question and let the system valuate each audit question to see if it meets the audit standards or not. If not, then corrective/pre- ventive actions are put in place and their progress monitored. The audit is then valu- ated to see if it complies with the predefined audit clearance/passing criteria or not. All stakeholders sign off on the audit, which signals its completion, and finally an audit report is generated. We’ll look at each of these steps in the following sections. © 633 14.3 Business Processes

sections.title: Release Audit Plan
sections.en: 14.3.1 Release Audit Plan Referring back to Figure 14.3, first the default or current system status of an audit plan is created. Figure 14.10 shows the Status tab, in which you choose Set to set the status of the audit plan to Release. If you choose Set Approval Requirement, then the system offers options to either approve or reject the audit plan. Once the audit plan is approved, you then have to release it. Save your entries. Figure 14.10 Releasing the Audit Plan

sections.title: Release Audit
sections.en: 14.3.2 Release Audit Similar to releasing the audit plan, you perform the same steps to release the audit in the Status tab of the audit. When you release the audit plan as well as the audit, the sys- tem enables more options via which you can maintain further details of the audit. With an audit released for further working—that is, the actual audit—you can valuate a question or question list.

sections.title: Valuate Question
sections.en: 14.3.3 Valuate Question Figure 14.11 shows the Valuation view of a question. In the Valuation area, selecting the Not Relevant checkbox makes this question irrelevant for valuation during audit calcu- lation. To valuate a question, enter No. of Points as “50”, and choose Valuation Entered to confirm that you want to valuate the question. Remember that you set the mini- mum number of points for this question must as 90.0. The system automatically marks the question as Action Required. You can also add different texts about the 14 Audit Management 634 action by choosing ID from the dropdown and then entering the long text in the pro- vided text box. You can also see the Corrective and Preventive Action icon right below the question. Figure 14.11 Question Valuation At this time, the system only updates the status of the question as either valuated or not valuated. This is shown in Figure 14.12 with a red circle icon or a green square icon to denote that the system has completed the valuation of the question. Figure 14.12 Question Valuated After you valuate a question, and depending on the company’s business process, you can create a corrective or preventive action to attend to the failed audit question and provide another opportunity to valuate the question. If you have more audit questions, then you need to valuate each and every individual audit question so that during audit valuation, the system valuates the entire questions list too. © 635 14.3 Business Processes

sections.title: Create Corrective and Preventive Action
sections.en: 14.3.4 Create Corrective and Preventive Action During an audit, you can determine follow-up activities based on the results of an audit, including actions to determine the necessity of a subsequent audit, or corrective, preventive, and improvement actions. You can assign persons responsible, monitor the subsequent steps, and verify the effectiveness of all actions by recording and reporting on the progress data. A corrective and preventive action defines the preven- tive measure that the audit team will put in place to ensure reduction or elimination of the cause of the defect and also prevent it from happening in the future. In the screen in Figure 14.11, choose Corrective and Preventive Action for a question so that the screen in Figure 14.13 appears. Figure 14.13 Corrective/Preventive Action Here, enter the action identification and its description of the correction/preventive action. In the Basic Data tab, enter the Planned Start Date and the To Be Completed By date. At this time, the system status of the action is Created. You need to continue updating the status of the action so that the system can valuate the question and, even- tually, the question list.
