You do this in the next step by choosing Status, and the screen in Figure 14.14 appears. Figure 14.14 1 shows the Status tab of the action, in which you choose Set, and then from the dropdown that appears, choose Open. The system sets the action’s status to Outstanding. In the Basic Data tab, enter the Actual Start Date and Actual End Date, as well as the Level of Completion as a percentage (%). Then, in the next step, choose Status. First con- firm the status, and then set the status as Complete 2. When you or the person assigned to complete the corrective/preventive action per- forms the correction/preventive action, you can update this information accordingly in the system. You update the information by adding relevant details in the different texts available for a corrective/preventive action. 14 Audit Management 636 Figure 14.14 Status Updates for Corrective/Preventive Action Note You can integrate a digital signature in either or both steps of corrective/preventive action—that is, at the time of confirming an action or on its completion. Chapter 3 dis- cusses digital signatures.

sections.title: Valuate Audit
sections.en: 14.3.5 Valuate Audit Choose Valuate in the screen in Figure 14.15 for the Audit, and the system updates all fields in the Audit Result area. The system calculates the Deg. of Fulfill (degree of fulfill- ment) at 50%. This is because you valuated the audit question with 50 points. Notice that the system assigns the Rating as 02 Medium Risk and assigns the Overall Assesst (assessment) as 0 Failed. Because the overall assessment of the audit has failed, the sys- tem automatically selects the Subsequent Audit Required checkbox, which you can manually override. If you choose not to override this, then you can enter the date of the next audit. Figure 14.16 shows more audit questions on the left side, with audit question NSA - Second Audit. Notice the red circle traffic light icon that denotes the question Overall Supplier’s Compliance Assessment failing to meet the minimum result. Note You can integrate digital signatures in the Signature step in Figure 14.16. Choose Sig- nature; because there is no digital signature in audit management, the system locks all fields from further changes. Refer to Chapter 3 where digital signature is covered in detail. © 637 14.3 Business Processes Figure 14.15 Audit Valuation Figure 14.16 Audit Valuation with More Questions Figure 14.16 shows that Deg. of Fulfill. does indeed improve to 100%, and has the Overall Assesst. status as 1 Passed (see the Minimum Result field in Figure 14.15, where you maintained 90%). Figure 14.17 shows the audit results of a third audit with an overall score of 95.0%. With your audit valuation complete, you can now create or sign the audit report. 14 Audit Management 638 Figure 14.17 Third Audit Valuation

sections.title: Audit Report
sections.en: 14.3.6 Audit Report In Figure 14.17, choose Create Report, and a popup appears to confirm that you want to print the audit report. Figure 14.18 Audit Report © 639 14.3 Business Processes Choose Yes, and Figure 14.18 appears, showing the standard audit form that contains all the relevant details of the audit after its valuation. You can engage an ABAP resource to custom-develop the audit report to meet your company’s business needs. Scroll down or press (Page Down), and the screen in Figure 14.19 appears, showing more details about the question list or question. It also contains the valuation and the correc- tive/preventive action that you need to take to ensure compliance with audit require- ments. Finally, when you complete the audit, you can set the audit’s status to Complete, and the system disables all fields to prevent any further changes or updates to it. Figure 14.19 Audit Questions in Audit Report 14 Audit Management 640

sections.title: Productivity Tools and Audit Monitor
sections.en: 14.4 Productivity Tools and Audit Monitor Managing and maintaining the enormous amount of audit data can be a herculean task. To support planning, scheduling, monitoring, and data entry efforts, audit man- agement provides several productivity tools and an audit monitor.

sections.title: Audit Plan in Microsoft Project
sections.en: 14.4.1 Audit Plan in Microsoft Project Audit management facilitates the planning and data entry efforts required to manage large amounts of information, especially when there are several different audit types scheduled and you need complete and overall scheduling visibility of some or all of them. Audit management integrates with Microsoft Project, so you can leverage a large number of Microsoft Project’s planning tools to optimize your audits. In the screen in Figure 14.20, choose an Audit Plan, and then choose Graphical Time Scheduling. This triggers the system to open Microsoft Project and then display the scheduling details of the audit plan in Microsoft Project. You can make changes to your audit plan in Microsoft Project, and on saving, the system automatically updates all scheduling information in audit management. Figure 14.20 Audit Plan in Microsoft Project Configuration Tip You can completely map the fields between audit management and Microsoft Project so that during upload or download, the system is able to place the correct data in the relevant fields. For field mapping between the programs, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Audit Management  Audit Definition  System Adjustment  Microsoft Project Interface.

sections.title: Import and Export Audits
sections.en: 14.4.2 Import and Export Audits You can import (upload) or export (download) your audits using XML format, which eventually saves you from redundant data entry efforts. To import or upload an audit, use menu path More  Audit Component  Import. To export or download your audit to your local drive, use menu path More  Audit Component  Export. © 641 14.4 Productivity Tools and Audit Monitor Tips and Tricks When you export the XML file, you can use Microsoft Excel to open it. On completing data entry and all tasks for audit in Microsoft Excel, you save the file in the XML format, which you can then import again into the SAP S/4HANA system.

sections.title: Audit Monitor
sections.en: 14.4.3 Audit Monitor The audit monitor provides different search possibilities for all audit components on the basis of various search criteria. In the audit monitor, you can, for example, deter- mine the number of outstanding corrective or preventive actions, display all audits or question lists, and determine which audit plans exist for a certain time period. The audit monitor accesses all data that was created in the system in the context of audit management. Access the audit monitor using Transaction PLM_AUDITMONITOR or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Audit Management  Start Audit Monitor. Figure 14.21 shows the initial screen of the audit monitor, wherein you can enter the informa- tion as selection criteria so that the system brings up only the relevant results. Figure 14.21 Audit Monitor 14 Audit Management 642 You can search for relevant audits, audit plans, or their items from a large number of search criteria, such as the status of audit items or the person(s) who created or changed the audit items. Select the Detailed Search (Show and consider specific search criteria) checkbox located further down the same screen so that the system brings up even more selection options, such as dates and audit types, for you to choose from. Entering relevant dates is also helpful when you want to know which audits are due within the specified dates. Select the Audit Plans radio button, and then enter “*NSA*” as the Identification. Choose Execute or press (F8), which brings up Figure 14.22. This screen consists of all the previously entered (or calculated) details, including the audit results, the audit type, and the dates when it was first created and then subsequently changed. With many evaluation tools available, you can add new fields, change layouts, get graphical presen- tations of audit objects, or even get a printout of the audit report. Figure 14.22 Audit Monitor Worklist

sections.title: Audit Inspection: Inspection Type 07
sections.en: 14.5 Audit Inspection: Inspection Type 07 Audit management has its own advantages, especially its application in managing diverse and different types of audits, which cater to almost all types of businesses. However, it doesn’t integrate with supplier evaluation for quality scoring. To attend to the business processes in which supplier audit scoring also forms an integral part of supplier evaluation vis-à-vis the quality scores from the usage decision, you can lever- age inspection type 07 with inspection origin 07 (supplier audit). Your inspection plan for the inspection lot can consist of master inspection characteristics that you use to record audit results, just as you use questions in audit management. The inspection plan’s usage should be set to 3 (universal). Finally, the usage decision for the inspection lot updates the quality scores. Inspection type 07 isn’t stock-relevant. Note Refer to Chapter 19 to see how you can influence the quality score of the usage decision of inspection type 07 in the supplier evaluation. © 643 14.5 Audit Inspection: Inspection Type 07 Access the screen shown in Figure 14.23 through Transaction QA01, and on the initial screen, enter Material “RM124”, Plant “1710”, and Insp. Lot Orig. “07” (Supplier Audit). Here, you can enter the supplier, and with the complete QM master data already in place, the system should be able to calculate the sample size. An important aspect to note here is that the system doesn’t ask for or have the option to enter an inspection quantity for inspection type 07, whereas during normal manual inspection creation (inspection type 89), the system does ask for the inspection quantity’s information. Similarly, because this inspection type is specific to supplier audit only, the Supplier field is available for input, not Customer. Figure 14.23 Audit Inspection: Inspection Type 07 The remaining steps of this manually created inspection lot are the same—that is, results recording, defects recording (if any), and usage decision. Tips and Tricks You can configure the system to make the Supplier field mandatory during inspection lot creation. This trick applies to just about any field that you want to control, such as display, input, mandatory, or highlight. Follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Environment  Tools  System Modification  Adapt Field Selection. In the Module Pool field, enter “SAPLQPL1”, choose Change, and then choose Inspection Lot. Make the QALS-LIFNR field a manda- tory (Required) entry by selecting the radio button available next to the field. 14 Audit Management 644 If you aren’t sure which module pool or program to use or the technical name or details of a field, then place the cursor on the specific field, press (F1), and choose Technical Information. The system displays both the Program Name (i.e., the module pool) and the Screen Field, which is the technical name of that specific field.

sections.title: Configuration Basics
sections.en: 14.6 Configuration Basics Now that you’re familiar with how to set up master data and run the business processes in audit management, the following sections cover the configuration objects that are specific to audit management. As mentioned earlier, we recommend that you also read the configuration basics of FMEA in Chapter 16; FMEA’s configuration basics highly overlap with those of audit management.

sections.title: Audit Usage
sections.en: 14.6.1 Audit Usage An audit usage logically separates various types of audits in the company. These can be safety audits, environmental audits, or data security audits. Configuring the relevant audit usages that meet the company’s business needs eventually helps in reporting. When you configure an audit type, the system prompts you to enter its audit usage. To create an audit usage, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Audit Management  Audit Definition  Audit Usage. Figure 14.24 consists of several audit usages already available that you can use, or you can create a new one by choosing New Entries and entering the usage and the description of the audit usage. Figure 14.24 Audit Usage

sections.title: Audit Type
sections.en: 14.6.2 Audit Type At the time of setting up an audit, some of the first information that the system requires from the business user is audit type. An audit type can be a system, product, process, or other. You can also define an audit type to meet your company’s business © 645 14.6 Configuration Basics needs. However, note that with every audit type, you also have to assign it an audit usage. To set up an audit type, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Audit Management  Audit Definition  Audit Type. Figure 14.25 shows an audit type consisting of several audit types. Notice audit type 51, audit usage 50 (quality audit), and the audit category system. This is the same audit type you used while setting up master data for audit management, as well as covering its business processes. Choose Aud.Type 51, and then choose Details so that the screen in Figure 14.26 appears. Figure 14.25 Audit Types Overview Figure 14.26 Detailed Screen of Audit Type 51 Figure 14.26 shows the Audit Type 51, Audit Usage 50 Quality Audit, and Audit Category 3 Process. Here, you can also control whether an audit must first go through an approval process (through a system update status) before the business user can release it by making a selection in the App. Requirement field. 14 Audit Management 646 Next, choose Input Fields for Audit Type (on the left side of Figure 14.25), and the screen in Figure 14.27 appears. The audit usage is the same as you previously configured in Sec- tion 14.6.1. Figure 14.27 Input Fields Control for Audit Type Here, you can assign the table and field name within the table so that these are avail- able at the time of creating an audit. Choose Settings for Role on the left side of Figure 14.25 shown earlier, and the screen in Figure 14.28 appears. Figure 14.28 Settings for Role in Audit Type In Figure 14.28, you define the roles that will let you have control over who can be part of the audit team. The roles that you assign here are then available in the Participants(s) tab of an audit.

sections.title: Digital Signature
sections.en: 14.6.3 Digital Signature You can integrate digital signatures into several steps in audit management, including while evaluating an audit, completing an audit, confirming action, and completing pre- ventive/corrective action. In Figure 14.25 shown earlier, choose Audit Type 51 and then Digital Signature from the left side of the screen. Here, you assign one or more already configured digital signa- ture strategies in some or all of the following four areas:  Evaluate Audit: Individual signature  Complete Audit: Multiple signatures strategy © 647

sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 14.7 Summary  Confirm Corrective Action: Multiple signatures strategy  Complete Corrective Action: Individual signature Note Refer to Chapter 3 where digital signature is discussed in detail. If there’s a business need, then digital signature can be integrated in the audit management process.

sections.title: Audit Trigger
sections.en: 14.6.4 Audit Trigger The option to enter an audit trigger is available at the time of creating an audit. An audit trigger provides the business user with the option to define why an audit is nec- essary. An audit trigger can be a regular annual or quarterly audit, or a process improvement initiative. To create an audit trigger, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Audit Management  Audit Definition  Audit Trigger. In the screen that appears, evaluate whether the already available audit triggers meet your company’s business needs. If not, create a new one, which then becomes available at the time of creating an audit. 14.7 Summary In this chapter, we showed you how to map and implement actual audit processes and integrate them in the QM area of an SAP S/4HANA system. You can also take advantage of the system to calculate audit results, as well as have a question list to help you with your audit management initiative. The audit monitor is a powerful tool to monitor and keep track of your various audit objects. Inspection types for supplier audits help you integrate the results from the usage decision with the supplier evaluation. The produc- tivity tools enable you to leverage Microsoft Office products that completely integrate with audit management. The next chapter discusses stability studies. ©

sections.title: Integration Workflow
sections.en: 15.1 Integration Workflow The stability study with a material requires a decent knowledge of four different SAP S/4HANA areas: quality management (QM), production planning (PP), plant mainte- nance (PM), and materials management (MM). It’s in the QM area that the stability 15 Stability Study 650 study with (or without) a material is performed, along with several associated activi- ties, such as results recording and usage decision. In the actual business process of conducting a stability study, all the related depart- ments of the company come together to contribute to their share of this endeavor (sta- bility study). This includes, but isn’t limited to, the decision-making process to determine which of the following options you’ll choose:  Proceed with the full-fledged stability study, or cancel it after the initial test  Revise the testing schedule of storage conditions, or shorten or prolong it  Cancel the stability study, or simply “deactivate” it for a limited time to be reacti- vated later Figure 15.1 provides a better picture of the stability study workflow. Figure 15.1 Stability Study Workflow The stability study with (or without) a material draws its fundamental concept from the notification in QM. In fact, the first step toward creating a stability study begins with cre- ating a special QM notification that’s available for stability studies only. Hence, this chap- ter will intermittently refer to stability studies with either a material or a notification. Create stability study Start Initial test Continue stability study? Stability planning Stability test Finish stability study End No Yes © 651

sections.title: Master Data
sections.en: 15.2 Master Data For the stability study, inspection types 16, 1601, and 1602 are applicable. Table 15.1 explains each of the three inspection types in the material master and their roles in the stability study. We’ll cover the actual applications of all three inspection types in this chapter. Note The inspection plans’ usage for all three inspection types is 9 (Material Check). 15.3 Stability Study for a Material We’ll now cover every step of the stability study with a material. We’ll also address all the options and choices available in the Action Box of the stability study with a mate- rial. To facilitate the understanding and learning process, we’ll move in a logical order so that it’s easier to comprehend the relationship between each sequential action during the stability study for a material. Inspection Type Inspection Type Description Role of Inspection Type in Stability Study 16 Inspection for Storage Condition (Stabi) This inspection type ensures the creation of the inspec- tion lot for the storage condition of the stability study. Once the sample is stored in the defined storage condi- tion, it’s imperative that the sample is periodically inspected to assess that its physical and chemical condi- tions meet the desired requirements. Creation of an inspection lot is generally ensured through a testing schedule, which stipulates pre- defined, periodic, and regular inspections during the stability study. 1601 Initial Test (Stability Studies) This inspection type ensures that before the actual sta- bility study starts, the business process owner approves the initial test for the sample. On approval or otherwise, a decision is made to continue or not continue with the stability study. 1602 Manual Insp. Lot for Storage Cond (Stab) This inspection type ensures that at any given point in time, if there’s a need to create an inspection lot for a storage condition (and which deviates from the testing schedule), then the necessary provision is in place. Table 15.1 Inspection Types for Stability Study 15 Stability Study 652

sections.title: Create Stability Study with a Material
sections.en: 15.3.1 Create Stability Study with a Material To create a new stability study with a material, use Transaction QST01 or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Stability Study  Stability Study  Create. On the initial screen for creating a stability study, enter the notification type QS, which is for stability study with a material, and an internal notification/stability study number that the system generates, which in this example is 800000004. Then, press (Enter) to go to the screen in Figure 15.2. As previously explained, a stability study is a special form of quality notification. Further, the notification type QS is available in the standard SAP model company provided by SAP. Note If you need to work with a stability study without a material, then the available notifi- cation type in the IDES system is QR. In a stability study without a material, there is no reference to a material or its associated batch number. However, all the steps that we cover in this chapter for a stability study with a material are equally applicable to a sta- bility study without a material (but without direct reference to a material or batch number). The system also offers another notification type, QT, which is for a stability study trial. This stability study type uses predefined and preconfigured building blocks consisting of planning data to facilitate the stability study. In Figure 15.2, enter Material “2234” and Plant “1710”. Because this material is batch- managed, the system requires the batch number, along with the storage location. We assign these as 121 and 171A, respectively. Prior to starting the stability study with a material, you can create a batch for this material and plant with Transaction MSC1N. If you’ve maintained the date of manufacturing and expiration date (shelf-life expiration date/best-before date [SLED/BBD]) of the batch, then these will also automatically appear in the stability study screen. The entire chapter will refer to not just this mate- rial but also its corresponding batch number, 121, available at storage location 171A. Note The focus of this entire chapter is on the tasks shown in the Action Box on the right side of Figure 15.2. We’ll cover each of these tasks in detail. We’ll cover the first two steps of the Action Box, Display Objects for Study and Display Stability History, at the end of the chapter. This approach will make sense when we’ve performed necessary actions for the stability study and the relevant information becomes available in the first two objects of the Action Box. Let’s start with step number three of the Action Box, which is Create Initial Sample, and then proceed with each step of the Action Box in sequential order. © 653 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.2 Detailed Screen of Stability Study with Material and Action Box Note We’ll refer to Figure 15.2 and/or the Action Box in the rest of this chapter, unless other- wise mentioned.

sections.title: Initial Sample
sections.en: 15.3.2 Initial Sample Before an actual stability study begins, it’s important to create an initial sample of the stability study. The initial sample is the physical sample of the stability study. This physical sample goes through the regular QM tasks of results recording, defects record- ing (if any), and usage decision to validate the process and decide whether a full-fledged stability study should continue or not. Just as with normal inspection, the initial sam- ple for the stability study also contains comprehensive details related to sample size, packing, sample location, and storage condition. In the following sections, we’ll show how to create, change, and then confirm an initial sample. An initial sample needs to be confirmed to proceed further with the stability study. 15 Stability Study 654 Create Choose Create Initial Sample from Action Box to go to Figure 15.3. Here, enter the details that relate to sample container, sample quantity, storage condition, and sample loca- tion. Choose Save and Change Notification. On saving, the system creates a physical sample, which in this example is 900000026. Because this is the initial sample, this ref- erence of the initial sample remains available throughout the entire process of the cov- ering stability study with material. Figure 15.3 Creating Initial Sample Change If you need to make any changes after creating an initial sample, then choose Change Initial Sample from Action Box, as shown in Figure 15.4. Notice that in change mode, the system has already created a physical sample 900000026 with the status set as created (CRTD). Make any desired changes, such as changing the sample size from a quantity of 3 (as first defined in Figure 15.3) to 2 PC. Choose Save and Change Notification in Figure 15.4. Doing so saves the changes you’ve made and brings you back to the change notifi- cation (stability study) screen. © 655 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.4 Changing Initial Sample Confirm The next step is the confirmation of the initial sample. A confirmation validates that the initial sample can form the basis of proceeding further with the stability study. To confirm an initial sample, choose Confirm Initial Sample in Action Box to go to Figure 15.5. This screen contains the previously entered information of the initial sample. Notice the option to enter the No. (number) of Labels for the initial sample. You can print these labels and physically paste them onto the physical samples’ containers. Enter the number of labels to be printed as “3”, and choose Save and Change Notifica- tion to go to the screen shown in Figure 15.6, which is a popup that appears with the pro- vision to add or update additional information and relates to the confirmation of the initial sample. Enter or update the information, and choose Continue. The system accordingly updates the status of the physical sample of the initial test to REL (released). 15 Stability Study 656 Figure 15.5 Confirmation of Initial Sample Figure 15.6 Additional Details for Confirmation of Initial Sample

sections.title: Bill of Materials
sections.en: 15.3.3 Bill of Materials Because we’re creating the stability study with a material, the system allows you to enter details of the components used in the stability study. These components are in the form of a bill of materials (BOM). A BOM contains the details of an individual com- ponent, together with its quantity. The following sections will discuss how to assign a BOM to a stability study and be able to maintain it subsequently. © 657 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Assign Choose Assign Bill of Material in Action Box to go to Figure 15.7. Figure 15.7 Assign Bill of Materials Here, the system also allows entering a BOM of another material. Notice that the Usage of the BOM in Figure 15.7 is defined as a stability study. This usage prevents the BOM from being used in the normal production process. The stability study usage of a BOM has limited functions because material is still going through the development, trial, and testing phases. When the stability study is successful, you can change the BOM usage to 1, which is for production. Choose Assign Bill of Material. Tips and Tricks We suggest creating a BOM for the material and its usage 8 beforehand so that you can assign it in this step. To create a material BOM, use Transaction CS01. This is an integration point between QM and PP. Further, to ensure that Usage 8 is allowed in Figure 15.7, make the necessary entry in Transaction OS21 if it doesn’t exist. Maintain After the initial assignment of a material BOM to the stability study, you can also make further changes to it if needed. These changes can include, for example, the deletion of a BOM component or a change in the quantity. To make changes in the BOM, choose Maintain Bill of Material in Action Box to go to the change screen for the BOM shown in Figure 15.8. Notice that one of the components is 15 Stability Study 658 RM20, with a quantity of 10 PC (pieces). If needed, you can change the quantity of this component or even add a new component. Choose Save to save the BOM. Figure 15.8 Changes to Bill of Materials

sections.title: Initial Test Inspection Lot: Inspection Type 1601
sections.en: 15.3.4 Initial Test Inspection Lot: Inspection Type 1601 After the confirmation of the initial sample, the next important step is the creation of an inspection lot for the initial test in the stability study. An inspection lot for the ini- tial test automatically creates an inspection lot of inspection type 1601. Warning Until the initial sample is confirmed, you can’t create an inspection lot for the initial test of the stability study. The system checks that the physical sample has the released (REL) status, and if so, allows inspection lot creation. This shows the importance of fol- lowing the sequence of steps given in Action Box. In Action Box, choose Initial Test Inspection Lot to go to the screen in Figure 15.9. Notice that the physical sample 900000026 is the same physical sample that we’ve worked on in the previous steps. The inspection lot, which the system creates, is inspection type 1601. You can manually assign the task list Group “7” and Group Counter “1”, which we previously covered in Section 15.2, as part of the stability study master data. Choose Inspection Lot in Figure 15.9 to create an inspection lot and to go to the screen in Figure 15.10. Figure 15.10 shows the selection screen for master inspection characteristics that the system brings up for inspection lot results recording and usage decision. The master inspection characteristics are taken from the inspection plan that was previously avail- able as a part of the QM master data. © 659 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.9 Creating Inspection Lot for Initial Test Inspection Figure 15.10 Option to Flexibly Select or Change Details of Master Inspection Characteristics Notice the flexibility you have in selecting the relevant master inspection characteris- tics, which are then available for results recording and usage decision. At this stage, you can also change the other details, such as lower or upper limits or even the target value of any master inspection characteristic. For this example, first choose Select All to select all the master inspection characteristics, and then choose Copy All to copy all the master inspection characteristics to the inspection lot. With this step, the system creates a new inspection lot for the initial test of the stability study with inspection type 1601. For this example, this inspection lot number is 160000000005. 15 Stability Study 660 Now that the system has created an inspection lot for the initial conditions for the sta- bility study, we’ll briefly discuss the associated QM activities, such as results recording and usage decisions, before we return to Action Box to cover the remaining available options.

sections.title: Inspection Process for an Initial Sample: Results Recording and Usage
sections.en: 15.3.5 Inspection Process for an Initial Sample: Results Recording and Usage Decision Because the results recording and usage decisions are standard QM activities, we’ll quickly walk you through how the system incorporates all the information and details from the stability study into the newly created inspection lot, as well as the role of inspection points. To record results, use Transaction QE01, and on the initial screen, enter Inspection Lot “160000000005” and Operation “0010”. Press (Enter), and the system shows the Assigned Insp. Pnt button. Click once, and the system automatically assigns physical sample 900000026. Figure 15.11 appears after we’ve entered the results of operation 0010, and it also con- tains details of physical sample 900000026 against the inspection lot. Save the entries and repeat the same steps for operation 0010 so that the screen in Figure 15.12 appears. This step highlights the importance of the inspection points that we previously covered. Figure 15.11 Initial Screen for Results Recording of Inspection Lot Choose the Samples Overview for Material button located at the bottom-right side of the screen shown in Figure 15.13, which shows not just the initial phyicsal sample 900000026 associated with this inspection lot but also other additional details. © 661 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.12 Results Recording of Inspection Lot Figure 15.13 Usage Decision of Inspection Lot For the usage decision, use Transaction QA11, and on the initial screen, enter Inspection Lot “160000000005”. In the screen in Figure 15.13, enter the usage decision code (UD Code) as “0010” and “STABI” to accept and approve the results of the initial test inspec- tion for the stability study. This usage decision code selection also confirms that we’ll proceed with executing the stability study. Choose the Samples tab to go to the screen in Figure 15.14. 15 Stability Study 662 Figure 15.14 Detailed Screen for Physical Samples of Inspection Lot Figure 15.14 shows the detail screen for physical sample 900000026 and its corre- sponding operation used in the initial test inspection lot for the stability study. Save your entries. You then receive a message confirming the successful completion of the initial test for notification type 800000004. So far, we’ve created, confirmed, and approved the initial test inspection lot for the sta- bility study by means of results recording and usage decision. Let’s return to the remaining steps and options available in Action Box for a stability study with a mate- rial.

sections.title: Change Notification
sections.en: 15.3.6 Change Notification On saving the original notification 800000004 and performing other activities such as results recording or usage decision, you can use the change notification option to return to the stability study with a material. To change the notification, use Transaction QM02 or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Stability Study  Stability Study  Change. On the initial screen for chang- ing the notification type, enter the Notification “800000004”, and press (Enter). This brings us back to the screen in Figure 15.2, but this time in change mode.

sections.title: Complete Initial Test
sections.en: 15.3.7 Complete Initial Test In Action Box, choose Complete Initial Test. This confirms and saves the results of the initial test of the inspection lot. © 663 15.3 Stability Study for a Material

sections.title: Storage Conditions
sections.en: 15.3.8 Storage Conditions Because the inspection lot for the initial test was successful as well as approved, the next step is to specify the storage condition(s) to keep the physical samples in. In Action Box, choose Specify Storage Conditions. In the screen in Figure 15.15, enter the sample quantity for each storage condition. Figure 15.15 Define Storage Conditions of Stability Samples In this example, enter a sample quantity of 1 PC; each is stored in Stor.Cond. (the first column to the left) 00000001 with the text “Room Temperature 21°”, and in Stor.Cond. 00000002 with the text “Temperature 20°”. In addition, notice that the physical sam- ple 900000026 now has the REL (for released) status. Select both Stor.Cond. 00000001 and Stor.Cond. 00000002, and choose Save and Change Notification. Note Storage conditions are covered in Section 15.4.3. You must carefully evaluate all the storage conditions that you’ll need for the stability study, and ensure their availability accordingly. 15 Stability Study 664 The following sections discuss the storage conditions and storage locations associated with a stability study. Specify Additional Storage Condition You can define additional storage conditions if there is any such need during the stabil- ity study. Choose Specify Add. Storage Conds in Action Box to arrive at the screen in Figure 15.16. Figure 15.16 Defining Additional Storage Conditions Here, you have the option to incorporate an additional storage condition for your sam- ples for the stability study. When you’ve made the necessary changes, choose Save and Change Notification. In this example, we enter the sample location shown in Figure 15.16. Store Stability Samples To formally begin the stability study process, you need to store the physical samples in the specified storage conditions. On doing so, the system updates the status of physical © 665 15.3 Stability Study for a Material samples to REL (released). With this status of physical samples, the system enables inspection lot creation, as well as all other standard QM activities, such as results recording, defects recording, and usage decision. To place the stability sample in stor- age, and according to chosen storage conditions, choose Store Stability Samples in Action Box to go to Figure 15.17. Figure 15.17 Store Stability Samples in Storage Conditions Here, you update the storage date and sample location, along with the number of labels required for printing. Choose the line item of storage condition 00000001, and then choose Save and Change Notification. Notice that the physical sample at storage condi- tion 00000001 still has the status CRTD. As soon as you save, the system updates the status to REL to release the physical sample. For this example, the physical sample number is 900000027 (the first field shown at the top in Figure 15.16). Use Transaction QPR3 to display physical sample 900000027 and to confirm whether the system updated the information on the physical sample accordingly (see Figure 15.18). Here, the system updates the physical sample’s status to REL and automatically creates inspection lot 160000000007. Because two physical samples were placed in two different storage conditions, the sec- ond physical sample that the system automatically created is 900000028 and the associated inspection lot. 15 Stability Study 666 Figure 15.18 Inspection Lot with Inspection Type 1602 Delete Storage Conditions You can delete a storage condition when you no longer want to continue with a sample placed in a certain storage condition. Choose Delete Storage Conditions in Action Box to go to the screen shown in Figure 15.19. You can, for example, select storage condition 00000002 and choose Delete and Change Notification. Doing so will remove the sam- ple from the stability study. © 667 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.19 Delete Storage Condition

sections.title: Testing Schedule
sections.en: 15.3.9 Testing Schedule If the initial test for the stability study proves satisfactory, then the next step is to cre- ate a testing schedule to monitor the progress or the physical and chemical conditions of the stored samples in the storage conditions over a longer period of time. Setting up a testing schedule enables the system to automatically create inspection lots per the defined schedule to ensure the stability study’s timely results recording and usage decisions. The following sections discuss how to create and change a testing schedule of a stability study and how to complete the testing schedule once the stability study is either com- pleted or isn’t required anymore. Create In Action Box, choose Create Testing Schedule. In Figure 15.20, due to the number range settings, the system internally assigns the Maintenance Plan 700020000002, whereas the maintenance planning category (Maint. plan cat.) ST denotes that it’s applicable to the stability study. A maintenance plan holds and controls all the information related 15 Stability Study 668 to planning and scheduling activities, including automatic creation of inspection lots, on the due dates of inspections. Figure 15.20 Testing Schedule of Inspection for Storage Conditions The maintenance strategy QSTABI is assigned to maintenance plan 700020000002 and is configured to create a new inspection lot every month for the material undergoing the stability study. The Scheduling Period of 1 year (YR) denotes that the stability study will last for one year; the system will create the number of inspection lots accordingly. Finally, in this case, the system creates a monthly inspection lot of inspection type 16, which is the inspection for storage condition. This inspection type compares with inspection type 1601, which was specific to initial sample creation. Note The maintenance plan category is an object that we’ll cover in Section 15.4.7. In addition, because maintenance strategies have extensive use in the PM area of SAP S/4HANA, consider engaging a PM resource to set up the correct maintenance strategy for your stability study. This is an integration point between QM and PM in the stability study. Setting up a maintenance strategy is a business process and not a configuration step, but we’ll cover it in Section 15.4.8 to maintain the ongoing business processes flow and continuity of the stability study in this section. Change You can change the testing schedule of the stability study. This can be helpful when there’s a need to change the testing frequency of the physical samples. You can also use this option to enter any missing or incomplete information in the maintenance plan. © 669 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Choose Change Testing Schedule in Action Box. A popup appears, asking you to con- firm whether you’d like to make changes to the testing schedule. Choose Yes so that the system navigates to the screen in Figure 15.21. Figure 15.21 Maintenance Plan for Changes in Testing Schedule In Figure 15.21, update Group “7” and TL Group Counter “1” in the Inspection Plan area. If you receive an error when doing so, follow these two troubleshooting steps: 1. Use Transaction CWBQM (Engineering Workbench), and in the popup that appears, enter “Q_OPR_000000000010”, which will bring up operations details of the inspection plan. On the screen that appears, enter Material “2234”, Plant “1710”, Task List Type “Q”, Group “7”, and Group Counter “1”, and then choose Load Task Lists from the top menu bar. In the Headers General tab of the screen that appears (see Figure 15.22), assign the maintenance Strategy as “QSTABI”. You’ll have to scroll to the far right of the screen to find this field for assignment. 15 Stability Study 670 2. Select the first operation shown in Figure 15.22, and choose Task Lists  Maintenance Packages, and maintain the monthly packages that belong to Strategy QSTABI, as shown in Figure 15.23. Figure 15.22 Assigning the Maintenance Strategy to the Inspection Plan Figure 15.23 Assigning the Maintenance Package Both these settings in the inspection plan for material 2234 and plant 1710 correspond to the options selected in Figure 15.20 previously. Further, when you’ve made both set- tings in the inspection plan via Transaction CWBQM (the Engineering Workbench) and © 671 15.3 Stability Study for a Material not via the normal inspection plan’s Transaction QP02, where these options aren’t available, you’ll be able to assign group 7 and group counter 1 to the maintenance plan, as shown in Figure 15.22. Tips and Tricks You can also use Transaction IP02 to directly make changes to the maintenance plan (testing schedule). Enter the maintenance plan 700020000002 on the initial screen and press (Enter), and it takes you to Figure 15.21. Furthermore, you can use Transaction IP10 to schedule automatic inspection lot cre- ation, which is relevant for stability studies. On the initial screen of Transaction IP10, enter the relevant maintenance planning category and maintenance strategy. Complete When the testing schedule for the stability study is complete, proceed to update the same so that the system no longer automatically creates inspection lots. Alternatively, you can complete the testing schedule anytime, as deemed necessary. Choose Complete Test Scheduling in Action Box, and a popup appears, asking you to confirm whether you’d like to set the status to Testing Scheduling Completed and return to the stability study. Choose Yes.

sections.title: Inspection Lot for Inspection Type 16
sections.en: 15.3.10 Inspection Lot for Inspection Type 16 With the testing schedule now in place, the system automatically creates inspection lot(s) of inspection type 16 on due date(s). Warning The status of the physical sample is still CRTD (created). Unless the physical sample attains status REL (released), the system doesn’t create inspection lots. To set the phys- ical samples’ status under storage conditions to REL, refer to Section 15.3.2. Figure 15.24 shows the detailed screen of Inspection Lot 160000000006. Notice that this screen has Inspection Type 16, notification 800000004, maintenance plan 700020000002 (not shown but located further down the same screen), and the strat- egy for stability study STABI. The rest of the steps are all the same as in standard QM activities, such as results record- ing and usage decision, and we won’t repeat them here. 15 Stability Study 672 Figure 15.24 Automatic Creation of Inspection Lot by Testing Schedule To check and test whether the system will create the inspection lot per the testing schedule, follow these steps: 1. Store stability samples, as covered in Section 15.3.7, so that the physical samples attain REL status. The system creates inspection lots only for physical samples with the REL status. 2. Use Transaction IP10, and then on the initial screen, enter the maintenance plan. In this example, it’s “700020000002”. 3. On the next screen, choose the Manual Call button to prompt the system to manu- ally trigger inspection lot(s) creation. When the system asks for the date (in a Manual Call field in a popup), enter today’s date, as shown in Figure 15.25. 4. Choose the Scheduled calls tab in Figure 15.26 to see the monthly scheduled mainte- nance calls made. 5. Save your entries and check for the newly created inspection lot using Transaction QA32 for inspection type 16 to bring up the screen in Figure 15.24, shown earlier. © 673 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.25 Start Date of Maintenance Cycle Figure 15.26 Maintenance Plan 700020000002

sections.title: Print Labels
sections.en: 15.3.11 Print Labels You can print the labels of storage conditions with details and paste them on physical samples for quick and easy identification. To print labels, choose Print Labels in Action Box. In Figure 15.27, enter the number of labels you’d like to print for samples in storage conditions. For this example, enter “1” in the first column, select the line item, and choose Print and Change Notification. 15 Stability Study 674 Figure 15.27 Print Labels for Storage Conditions To send the print labels request to the printer spool, use Transaction SP02 or menu path System  Own Spool Requests (see Figure 15.28). Here, you see the list of spool requests for print jobs. Choose the Print Preview icon of spool number 13700, and the screen in Figure 15.29 appears. Figure 15.28 List of Spool Requests © 675 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.29 Labels Printing Note Consider engaging an ABAP consultant (programmer) to develop the layout/format of the physical sample’s label that meets your company’s business needs.

sections.title: Define the Start Date of the Study
sections.en: 15.3.12 Define the Start Date of the Study The start date of the stability study is the formal start of the stability study and the date for the system to automatically create all further testing schedules. In Action Box, choose Define Start Date of Study, and enter the start date for your stability study. Choose Save and Change Notification.

sections.title: Manual Inspection Lot for Storage Condition: Inspection Type 1602
sections.en: 15.3.13 Manual Inspection Lot for Storage Condition: Inspection Type 1602 At any point in time, you can also create a manual inspection lot for the storage condi- tion of physical samples of your stability study. The inspection type for manually cre- ated inspection lots is 1602. In Action Box, choose Manual Insp. Lot f. Stor. Cond., and the screen in Figure 15.30 appears. Here, you see that the system already has Inspection Lot 160000000006 placed under Stor.Cond. 00000001. This inspection lot is the same one that the system created through testing the schedule. Select the line item containing Inspection Lot 160000000006, placed under Stor.Cond. 00000001, and choose Create Manual Inspection Lot And Change Notification. When you do so, the screen in Figure 15.31 appears, in which the system automatically sug- gests inspection type 1602. For this example, however, enter “7” for Group and “1” for Group Counter, as well as short text, and choose Inspection Lot. This step brings up the screen in Figure 15.32 to help you select the master inspection characteristics. The rest of the steps are all the same that we’ve previously covered in this chapter, so we won’t repeat them. 15 Stability Study 676 Figure 15.30 Manual Creation of Inspection Lot for Storage Condition Figure 15.31 Manual Creation of Inspection Lot for Stability Study © 677 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.32 Manual Inspection Lot with Inspection Type 1602 On successful creation of the manual inspection lot of inspection type 1602, use Trans- action QA03 (or Transaction QA32) to display the same (see Figure 15.33). This screen contains details about the newly created Inspection Lot 160000000007, as well as details of the stability study, including physical sample 900000027, in the lower half of the screen (not shown). Figure 15.33 Display Manual Inspection Lot for Stability Study 15 Stability Study 678

sections.title: Change Storage Conditions
sections.en: 15.3.14 Change Storage Conditions The next available option is to assess whether you can still make changes to storage conditions after the release of physical samples and label printing. In Action Box, choose Change Storage Conditions. At this stage, only a few details of the physical samples are changeable, such as sample location, sample container, and sam- ple quantity. Select the line item for Stor.Cond. 00000001, and choose Save and Change Notifica- tion. If you don’t want to continue with a further stability study of a specific physical sample, you can deactivate or block storage conditions at any time. In Action Box, choose Deac- tivate Storage Conditions and then, on the Lock/Unlock Storage Condition screen, select the checkmark under the Block Indicator column to lock or unlock storage condi- tion(s). Finally, select the line item for Stor.Cond. 00000001, and choose Lock/Unlock Change Notification.

sections.title: Change Stability Study Status
sections.en: 15.3.15 Change Stability Study Status While performing all the steps, activities, and business processes in the stability study, the system correspondingly continues to update its status. The stability study statuses are available near the top of the screen (look for Notif. Status) on the main notification screen. Table 15.2 lists some of the statuses of the stability study. Status Status Description Status Status Description ACTV Stability Study Active SCDF Storage Condition Defined CRIS Create Initial Sample STOR Stability Sample Stored BOMA Bill of Material Assigned CRTS Create Testing Schedule ISCR Initial Sample Created TSCR Testing Schedule Created ISRL Initial Sample Released TSCO Testing Schedule Completed CRIL Create Initial Test STRT Start of the Study ILCR Initial Test Created COMP Study Completed COIL Initial Test Completed CANC Study Canceled DFSC Define Storage Condition INAC Study Inactive Table 15.2 Selected Statuses of Stability Study © 679 15.3 Stability Study for a Material The following are some of the available options in a stability study:  Deactivate Stability Study You can also temporarily deactivate the stability study, if there is any such business need. This may be the case when you want to temporarily put the entire stability study project on hold. In Action Box, choose Deactivate Stability Study. In the ensuing popup, which asks you to confirm whether you want to deactivate the stability study, choose Yes to confirm your decision. A deactivated stability study also deactivates the testing schedule associated with the stability study.  Activate Stability Study Just like with deactivating, you can also reactivate an already deactivated stability study. In Action Box, choose Activate Stability Study. In the ensuing popup, which asks you to confirm whether you wish to activate the stability study, choose Yes to confirm your decision. A reactivated stability study also activates the testing sched- ule associated with the stability study.  Cancel Stability Study When there’s no further need to continue with a stability study, you can cancel it, if needed. When you cancel a stability study, the system locks the testing schedule, as well as the storage conditions of the sample(s). Further, you have to manually cancel the inspection lots. In Action Box, choose Cancel Stability Study, and in the ensuing popup, choose Yes to confirm your decision. For this example, we chose No because we still want to continue with the remaining steps of the stability study.  Complete Stability Study On completion of the stability study, it makes sense to update its status accordingly. In Action Box, choose Complete Stability Study, and in the ensuing popup, confirm your decision by choosing Yes. Note, however, that if there are any outstanding tests or other open inspection lots, the system doesn’t allow their completion unless you complete or cancel the inspection lots.  Remove Stability Samples On completion of the stability study, you can remove the samples of the stability study from their storage conditions. In Action Box, choose Remove Stability Samples to remove physical samples from storage conditions; even partial removal of physi- cal samples is possible. Select the first line item, and choose Save and Change Notification (see Figure 15.34). 15 Stability Study 680 Figure 15.34 Removing Stability Samples from Storage Conditions

sections.title: Display Stability Study
sections.en: 15.3.16 Display Stability Study With this, the standard end-to-end business process of the stability study and the options that it offers are complete. Now that you’ve learned how to set up a stability study and its business processes, we’ll show you how the system displays the stability study information in reports or workflows. Display Object for Study In Action Box, choose Display Objects for Study. This is now the very first item of the Action Box. Here, you’ll find a comprehensive audit trail that covers just about all the information that we presented in this chapter, as well as the sequence of activities that we undertook for the stability study with a material (see Figure 15.35). Tips and Tricks You can also choose the Display document button, located near the top of the stability study screen, to get a view of the stability study document flow. However, the details aren’t as comprehensive as you’ll find in the Display Objects for Study option. © 681 15.3 Stability Study for a Material Figure 15.35 Complete Trail of the Stability Study Display Stability Study History In Action Box, choose Display Stability History. Here, you’ll find the details of all the results of all the inspection lots that were created and for which results were recorded during the course of the entire stability study. This includes, for example, results of the initial test, the individual storage conditions in which the samples were kept, inspec- tion lots created, and their recorded results (see Figure 15.36 and Figure 15.37). Figure 15.36 Stability Study History of Initial Test 15 Stability Study 682 Figure 15.37 Stability Study History for Room Temperature at 21° Celsius

sections.title: Configuration Basics
sections.en: 15.4 Configuration Basics It should be a comfort knowing that the challenging task of configuring a stability study in SAP S/4HANA becomes easy based on all the knowledge and experience you’ve gained while configuring various other areas of QM. The main areas in which the stability study uses prior experience or knowledge are sample management, inspection lot creation and completion, notification creation with the catalog profile, and the information system, especially the info structure. This section begins by covering the configuration options available for the stability study. Wherever the information is previously covered, we’ll refer to the same without repeating the information. This includes, for example, the option to define and assign number ranges to a notification type, the catalog profile, and inspection lot creation from the configuration perspectives. This section does, however, cover the PP section of the bill of materials (BOM), as well as the PM portion of the testing schedule, with ref- erence to the maintenance plan category. © 683 15.4 Configuration Basics Let’s start with the configuration basics of the stability study. The basic data sets up the initial conditions to keep the initial samples of the stability study and includes packag- ing, sample management, and storage conditions. Tips and Tricks To save you the effort of defining all the parameters in any configuration object and also lessen the chances of errors, we suggest that you copy from one of the standard objects available and then make the desired changes to the newly created object. The copy function is available in all configuration objects. Look for the Copy As option.

sections.title: Primary Packaging
sections.en: 15.4.1 Primary Packaging Physical samples make use of primary packaging, not just during the initial sample but also in all activities in which samples are used or maintained. To set up primary pack- aging, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Basic Data  Define Primary Packaging. On the screen that appears for maintenance of the primary package for the stability study, create new entries as needed.

sections.title: Physical Sample Container
sections.en: 15.4.2 Physical Sample Container Refer to the configuration of a physical sample container in Chapter 10, Section 10.5.3. Create new entries as deemed necessary and save.

sections.title: Storage Conditions
sections.en: 15.4.3 Storage Conditions The storage condition is the physical condition in which a sample is stored. During the stability study, it’s important to identify the storage condition in which a sample is placed. To set up a storage condition, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Basic Data  Define Storage Conditions. On the screen that appears, you can create new entries as deemed necessary and save.

sections.title: Storage Locations
sections.en: 15.4.4 Storage Locations Refer to the configuration section of Chapter 10, Section 10.5.4, for defining storage locations.

sections.title: Bill of Material Usage
sections.en: 15.4.5 Bill of Material Usage A BOM usage during the stability study stipulates the controls of its usage for various functions. For example, a BOM usage may only be for costing purposes, while another usage may be for production. The controls are defined accordingly. To set up a BOM 15 Stability Study 684 usage, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Basic Data  Define Bill of Material Usage. BOM usage 8 is specifically available for the stability study. You’ll notice the various columns for usage 8, such as costing, production, and sales are marked with the No Entry indicator (the indicator is denoted by a - sign in all six columns).

sections.title: Samples for Stability Study
sections.en: 15.4.6 Samples for Stability Study Refer to the relevant sections of Chapter 10 on sample management for the following nodes in stability study configuration:  Define physical sample type (see Section 10.5.2)  Define number ranges (see Section 10.5.1)

sections.title: Testing Schedule Category
sections.en: 15.4.7 Testing Schedule Category In the testing schedule for a stability study, the configuration that you need to define is to call objects that the system should create on the date of the testing. Some of the call objects are PM notifications, PM orders, and QM inspection lots. Because we’d like the system to create a QM inspection lot on its due date, we’ll cover the desired settings in this section accordingly. To set up the testing schedule for a stability study, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Testing Schedule for Sta- bility Study  Define Testing Schedule Category. Figure 15.38 Maintenance Plan for Scheduling Type Figure 15.38 shows the initial screen to define details of the testing schedule. Notice that the Maint. plan cat. (maintenance plan category) ST is configured for the stability study and stipulates that the called object will be inspection lot creation. The Ref. © 685 15.4 Configuration Basics object (reference object) 0190 stipulates that the basis for trigging inspection lot cre- ation for the stability study will be the physical sample. To the extreme right of Figure 15.38, the number ranges are assigned. The number ranges can be both internal and external. Create new entries as deemed necessary and save.

sections.title: Maintenance Strategy
sections.en: 15.4.8 Maintenance Strategy Because we used maintenance strategy QSTABI in this chapter, we’ll cover its features to enable you to correlate the configuration with business processes. A maintenance strategy defines the frequency with which the system creates an inspection lot (the call object) on its schedule dates. Further, it also enables the business process owner to define the tolerance for early or late initiation or completion of specific inspection tasks. To set up the maintenance strategy for the stability study, use Transaction IP11 or fol- low menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Stability Study  Stability Planning  Strategy  Edit. You’ll see an initial screen to create or change a maintenance strategy. Choose QSTABI, and either double-click the QSTABI field or choose Details. This leads to the screen shown in Figure 15.39. Figure 15.39 contains the strategy unit that stipulates the time unit of measure that the system uses to create call objects. This unit of measure can be in hours, days, months, or years. Figure 15.39 Detailed Screen to Maintain Maintenance Strategy 15 Stability Study 686 A call horizon, defined as a percentage, enables the business process owner to control when the system creates a call object on its planned or due date. For example, a 0% call horizon means that as soon as the planned or due date of the call objects (in this case, inspection lots) is reached, the system immediately creates the inspection lot. Simi- larly, a 90% call horizon means that the system calls the object on a time horizon of 90% from the date of the next planned inspection lot creation. Other available options are how the system should respond when there are deviations between planned and actual tasks, such as inspection lot creation, its results recording, and its usage decision. You can define not only the tolerance for early or late completion in percentages, but also how much (as a percentage) the system should shift in dates when it finds devia- tions between planned and actual tasks. Choose Packages on the left side of Figure 15.40. This screen contains the cycle length, in months, that the system uses to calculate the next time it creates a call object (for the stability study, it’s an inspection lot) on its due date. Figure 15.40 Maintenance Packages

sections.title: Notification Type
sections.en: 15.4.9 Notification Type Because this chapter focuses on a stability study with a material, the corresponding QM notification type in SAP is QS. To view details of the notification type for the stability study, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Quality Noti- fication for Stability Study  Open Stability Study  Define Notification Type. On the ini- tial screen for various available notification types, choose Notification Type QS, which leads to the detailed screen in Figure 15.41 for notification type QS. Notice that the assigned catalog profile enables the availability of relevant tasks and activity codes to notification type QS. It’s also important to note that the Update Group (stats) field is set to 34, which updates the info structure for reporting purposes. We’ll cover info struc- tures in Chapter 18. © 687 15.4 Configuration Basics Figure 15.41 Notification Types

sections.title: Priority Type
sections.en: 15.4.10 Priority Type The priority type was previously covered during the notification creation section of configuration. Refer to Chapter 12, Section 12.8.5.

sections.title: Action Box
sections.en: 15.4.11 Action Box A highly important aspect of the stability study is to gain a comprehensive understand- ing of the Action Box, which is available to facilitate the business process side. It facili- tates the availability of all common business transactions in one place (in the stability study notification), meaning the user is no longer required to navigate to different screens and options. To navigate to Action Box for the stability study, follow menu path SAP IMG  Quality Management  Stability Study  Quality Notification for Stability Study  Perform Stability Study  Notification Functions  Define Action Box. On the initial screen to configure Action Box, choose Define Functions for the Action Box, and this leads to an overview of various notification types available in the system. Choose Notification Type QS. Here, the system automatically copies the catalog profile from Figure 15.41. You can add the relevant codes for tasks and activities so that, subsequently, the same becomes available on the notification screen of the stability study. Next, choose Activities in the dialog structure to see the screen in Figure 15.42, which shows an overview of all the activities that were visible in Action Box. Choose the first activity, Create Initial Sample, and then choose Details. The screen that appears shows the detailed view of the Create Initial Sample function. The important information to note is the assignment of the 15 Stability Study 688 function module to the creation of the initial sample. If a company has created a busi- ness-specific function module to cater to a unique process, then the consultant or the business process owner can assign it at this stage. Choose Dependent Follow-Up Functions in Figure 15.42, and you can add a new function for Dependent Follow-Up Function to the function or the Create Initial Sample action. Figure 15.42 Configuration View of Action Box

sections.title: Summary
sections.en: 15.5 Summary In this chapter, we covered a series of logical and sequential steps that can be used to cover just about all the business scenarios for implementing a stability study with a material in QM. In addition to highlighting the importance of the QM master data needed to implement a stability study, we also covered the cross-area integration of QM with PP, PM, and MM. Various possible scenarios and their implications on the sta- bility study were addressed. We also covered the configuration steps needed to successfully implement a stability study. A lot of information was drawn from previous experience of configuring and implementing various subareas of QM, such as sample management, inspection lot completion, and notification creation. The next chapter covers the processes in failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) and the control plan. ©

chapters.title: Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan

sections.title: Process Overview
sections.en: 16.1 Process Overview In this section, we’ll provide details to help you comprehend the actual steps involved in undertaking the FMEA initiative.

sections.title: Action Plan
sections.en: 16.1.1 Action Plan Companies can take the following 10 steps to chart a step-by-step approach to develop- ing an action plan using FMEA. With the exception of the first step, all the following steps are mapped in the SAP system: 1. Review existing business processes. Examine how each component of the process functions and its relation to the other items. For example, what process is currently in place to receive hazardous materials from a supplier, or which packing material does the company use to pack its fragile products? Use a detailed flowchart for each business process to review the chain of processes. When you review each component of the process with your team mem- bers, everyone gains a greater understanding of the entire process and how the var- ious components are interlinked. Using the process flowchart, you can assign applicable components to the relevant process owners who are performing specific functions in different departments of the company. Assigning applicable compo- nents to relevant process owners ensures accountability and visibility by clearly seg- regating and identifying their roles and responsibilities in the FMEA initiative. 2. List potential failure modes. List all the possible ways a product or process can fail to perform its function. Refer to previous documentation and other records to gain insight into the nature of pre- vious problems and how these were handled. 3. List potential effects of failure. Make detailed notes about the potential effects of failure. The effect directly relates to the failure of the specific process or component to perform its function. While noting details, record how the failure would affect other interconnected processes and functions. © 691 16.1 Process Overview 4. Assign severity rankings to each effect. Rank each effect based on how it would impact the entire value chain. This value chain can be a customer, dependent subsequent operations, or people involved in operating the process. The severity ranking is based on a relative scale ranging from 1 to 10, with 1 being extremely low and 10 being the highest severity. When assign- ing a severity to each effect, you can begin with a standard, general scale and then work closely with other team members to define a specific and relevant severity ranking for each effect. 5. Assign occurrence rankings to each cause. The occurrence ranking reflects the frequency or likelihood that a cause or failure mechanism will occur. Just like severity ranking, the occurrence ranking is also based on a scale of 1 to 10. Review the occurrence frequency by referring to the data and reports, such as the equipment failure record, customer complaints, or even the repair and rework reports. 6. Assign rankings to failure detection. Identify each process- or product-related control in place, evaluate the process of detecting failure, and assign a detection ranking to a failure on a scale of 1 to 10. A detection ranking of 1 indicates that detecting failure is certain, and a detection ranking of 10 means that detection of a failure isn’t possible or that no checks or controls are in place to detect the failure. 7. Calculate the RPN. As directed by the business process owner, the system automatically calculates the RPN, which quantifies the amount of risk of failure and helps prioritize improve- ment efforts. The RPN is determined by multiplying severity, occurrence, and detection. It’s always in the range of 1 to 1,000. The higher the RPN, the greater the risk. 8. Develop an action plan to reduce RPN. Lowering the RPN is made possible by focusing on lowering one or more of its three factors (severity, occurrence, or detection). For example, a reduction in detection ranking is accomplished by adding fail-safe processes in shutdowns, installing alarms or sensors, or ensuring timely preventive maintenance. 9. Implement the action plan. Assign people to each action and finalize a timeline for the completion of actions. A practical approach to adopt is the “who, what, and when” approach to implement the action plan. 10. Recalculate the resulting RPN. Recalculate the RPN after implementing the action plan to determine whether the desired RPN has been achieved. If it hasn’t, it may be necessary to repeat this series of steps or perhaps develop a new action plan. 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 692

sections.title: Failure Across Categories
sections.en: 16.1.2 Failure Across Categories FMEA categorizes risk of failure across three categories, including occurrence (how likely failure is to occur), severity (how big an impact it would have), and detection (how likely the failure is to be detected as soon as it occurs): Risk priority number (RPN) = Severity × Occurrence × Detection FMEA uses a 1–10 ranking for each factor, with 10 being very likely to occur, have a sig- nificant impact, or be detected. FMEA multiplies the three individual rankings of those three factors to come up with the RPN. The value of the RPN can be in the range of 1 to 1,000. The higher the RPN value is, the greater the possibility of failure is in a produc- tion or business process. Companies must then reduce the RPN as much as possible to prevent or eliminate failures. Companies can use FMEA in the SAP S/4HANA system to lower their RPNs by taking preventative and detection measures. The team that manages the FMEA predefines the valuation (on a scale of 1 to 10) for each of the three areas mentioned (occurrence, detection, and prevention) and the RPN benchmark that it wants to achieve. The FMEA team then undertakes practical actions, such as making design changes, placing visual signboards, and pasting labels to edu- cate the production or process users to adhere to given guidelines or conduct technical skills enhancement trainings. After performing these actions, the FMEA team updates the valuation of each of the three areas, and the system automatically recalculates the RPN. If the RPN is reduced to the benchmark level, the FMEA team calls this achieve- ment a success. If not, another round of practical actions is put in place, and the process to calculate new or reduced RPNs starts all over again.

sections.title: Closed-Loop Quality Approach
sections.en: 16.1.3 Closed-Loop Quality Approach The ability to create FMEA along with all its components and then integrate it with con- trols in the SAP system provides the added leverage of having all the critical informa- tion in one system (the SAP system). Further, FMEA also provides an option to create an extensive question list that acts as a validation tool to ensure that all questions were eventually validated with the correct/desired answers, and then it becomes possible for a company to achieve a reduced RPN. Figure 16.1 shows a step-by-step FMEA approach 1 in closed-loop quality management. It’s the direct outcome of complaints coming from customers 2 or analytics such as statistical process control monitoring 3 in production processes. Finally, you can leverage FMEA to incorporate important characteristics in an inspec- tion plan 4 for regular and consistent monitoring and control of characteristics that are critical to quality. Now that you have a better understanding of what FMEA is and does, let’s move on to setting up FMEA in the system. © 693

sections.title: Set Up
sections.en: 16.2 Set Up Figure 16.1 FMEA Workflow 16.2 Set Up You can access FMEA using Transaction QM_FMEA or menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Planning  Failure Mode and Effects Analysis  Cockpit (Figure 16.2). This screen shows some of the often hidden (or little-known) or unused produc- tivity tools and options available. Figure 16.2 1 shows the menu bar to create, change, copy, delete, expand, or shrink various FMEA elements. Another menu bar 2 offers options to switch between change or display FMEA, as well as make other relevant settings. With the third menu bar 3, you can attach files, refer- ence documents, and even web links to FMEA. Similarly, you can keep an eye on the alerts and messages 4 that are available at the top-right side of FMEA. Double-click the message icon, and details of the message appear at the bottom of the same screen 5. The final menu bar 6 offers options to view or print various FMEA elements. We sug- gest that you take time to explore the several tools and the menus that we’ve high- lighted in Figure 16.2. FMEA (product/ process) Statistical process control Zero-defect production Inspection plan Control plan Complaints (8D process) Quality notification Critical-to-quality characteristics Critical-to-quality characteristics Characteristics Defects Characteristics Defects Characteristics Defects Characteristics Defects Environment, health, and safety specification 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 694 Figure 16.2 Productivity Tools in FMEA Figure 16.3 divides the entire FMEA Cockpit into four distinct sections: 1 In the navigation area, the system provides the options to create new objects, such as an FMEA or question list. It also gives the flexibility to copy one FMEA item to another, delete an item within the FMEA, or even look for specific information within the FMEA. All these options are available via the icons available at the top-left side of Figure 16.3. Figure 16.3 Structure of FMEA © 695 16.2 Set Up 2 The work area of the screen is blank unless you’re already working on a specific FMEA. 3 The Worklist shows the FMEAs or other objects that you’ve worked on in the recent past and is available in the FMEA Cockpit’s history. To make more space in the FMEA Cockpit, you can hide the details shown in the lower-left side of the screen by choos- ing the Close button (the blue cross). 4 The cross-linking area helps to bring together all the FMEA items in one work area so that you can quickly create FMEA items. This option is especially helpful when you have several hierarchy levels in FMEA and need to create new links or navigate to any specific link. Tips and Tricks We’ll be taking the longer route of explaining each and every FMEA item in this chapter in detail, but you also can choose the Form button in Figure 16.3. Then, you can quickly and intuitively create all the items that we cover in this chapter 5. After reading the entire chapter and understanding all FMEA items, we suggest that you come back to Figure 16.3 to explore the available options and consider leveraging these productivity tools. Choose the New icon in Figure 16.4, and from the dropdown, you can create a new FMEA, a question list, or either of the two using a template. A template is a previously created FMEA or question list that you can use to save time and effort instead of man- ually entering all the details all over again. Figure 16.4 FMEA Cockpit to Create a New FMEA Choose FMEA from the dropdown list in Figure 16.4, and the system brings up the basic data view of the FMEA in Figure 16.5. On the right side of the screen, enter “REVO” for 16 Failure Mode and Effects Analysis and Control Plan 696 the FMEA field (for the rest of this chapter, we’ll use FMEA REVO as an example) and enter its Description. Notice the additional icons right next to the FMEA field that enable you to add additional notes or attachments for reference and record purposes. Figure 16.5 Basic Data Tab of FMEA The option to attach documents or notes is also generally available while you’re creat- ing all items of the FMEA.
